title: Canberra Catholic schools to increase fees for 2027
text:
Parents with children attending Catholic schools in the ACT have been notified of fee increases for next year.

Catholic Archdiocese of Canberra and Goulburn Education Limited (CACGEL), which operates 56 schools in the ACT and NSW, said its primary school fees would increase by 6 per cent next year.

Meanwhile, the fees at four of five Catholic secondary schools are set to increase by 7.5 per cent.

The exception is St John Paul II College in Nicholls, which saw fees raised for some year levels in 2025.

Instead, its fees will increase by 6 per cent, similar to primary schools.

The fees at Merici College in Braddon will rise by 7.5 per cent. (ABC News: Elise Pianegonda)

2027 will also be the final year the Catholic schools building levy, introduced in 2025, is set to increase, costing families $1,000 for the year.

For a Year 12 student at St Clare's College in Griffith, the total fee for 2027 — excluding the levy — will be $14,188, an increase of $991.

The fee increases come amid increased cost-of-living pressures, rising interest rates and an annual rate of headline inflation at 3.8 per cent in June.

Fees at St John Paul II College will only rise by 6 per cent after its fees rose for several year groups last year. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Catholic education office aiming to 'support every family in need'

In a statement, executive director David de Carvalho said CACGEL was trying to keep fees as low as possible.

"At the same time, we must ensure schools have the resources they need to meet the rising costs of providing a quality Catholic education," he said.

" Real decreases in per-student base government funding are putting increased pressure on fees. "

According to the 2026 ACT Census of Schools, more than 16,000 students attend Catholic schools in Canberra.

This year, the federal government's School Resourcing Standard base amounts were $14,467 for primary students and $18,180 for secondary students.

David de Carvalho says families with concerns about the fee rises can speak to their school's principal about remissions. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

CACGEL said it allocated all its government funding across its schools on a needs-based arrangement.

Mr de Carvalho said families who were concerned about fee increases could speak with school principals.

"We aim to support every family in need and believe no child should be denied a Catholic education because of an inability to pay fees," he said.

" Families can apply for fee remissions based on their particular circumstances. "

Most of Canberra's independent schools have not yet publicly released their fees for 2027.

Radford College's fee schedule indicates an 8.5 per cent increase for 2027, with a Year 12 student's tuition to cost $28,156.

Parents criticised the school last year for increasing its fees by 23 per cent.

title: The RBA just raised rates. It affects more than your home loan
text:
For the fourth time this year, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has lifted the cash rate by 0.25 of a percentage point in a bid to bring inflation under control.

While the RBA's decisions are most felt through mortgage repayments, their impact extends well beyond home loans.

Here's a breakdown of how the latest increase will affect households differently, depending on whether Australians are paying off a mortgage, renting, or relying on savings.

Where are we at with the cash rate?

To first understand how the cash rate impacts different parts of our hip pocket, let's take a step back.

The cash rate, set by the RBA, is Australia's official interest rate charged on unsecured overnight loans between banks.

In simple terms, it's how much it costs banks to borrow from each other. The RBA's decision to increase the official cash rate makes it more expensive for lenders to borrow money.

That means banks will almost certainly charge customers a higher interest rate to still make a profit because they are paying more to borrow the money in the first place.

On Tuesday, the RBA increased the cash rate to 4.6 per cent in an attempt to slow down inflation in the economy.

Commonwealth Bank head of Australian economics Belinda Allen says the central bank has lost its patience, given inflation has sat above the target band for most of the past six years.

"Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive," Ms Allen says.

"That tends to slow household spending and business investment, reducing some of the demand pressures in the economy and, over time, helping bring inflation back towards the RBA's 2–3 per cent target."

How the cash rate increase could affect you

Mortgages Read more Read more Rate rises are felt fastest, and most sharply, by Australians with variable-rate mortgages because banks typically pass on RBA increases in full. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver says the cash rate is the main tool steering borrowing costs and households should expect lenders to adjust quickly. "As we've seen with the first three hikes this year, the banks will likely announce a 0.25 per cent increase in their mortgage rates on the same day," Dr Oliver says. Ms Allen says households with a mortgage may lower spending or use savings to keep spending as a result of higher interest rates. "This cash flow channel is one way monetary policy works to impact demand in the economy," she says. Each 0.25 per cent rise in the cash rate adds roughly $91 per month to repayments on a $600,000 variable-rate loan with 25 years remaining. The four 2026 increases totalling 0.75 per cent have added approximately $360 per month for borrowers on a $600,000 loan. That equates to around $4,320 extra per year. Here's how much a September rate hike will cost borrowers, as well as the total monthly increase if rates go up for a fifth time in either November or December: Loan size Hike in September Total increase for 4 hikes Total increase for 5 hikes $600,000 +$91/month +$364/month +$456/month $750,000 +$114/month +$454/month +$570/month $1,000,000 +$152/month +$606/month +$759/month Source: Canstar It is not just existing mortgage borrowers hit by the rate rises though. For prospective buyers, Canstar estimates that the borrowing capacity of someone on an average full-time wage of $108,650 would be reduced by more than $47,000, while a couple both on average wages would see a reduction of nearly $95,000. If you are on a fixed-rate home loan, you won't see any changes. Those rates are locked in. But when the fixed term expires and rolls to a variable rate, the full impact of any rate cycle will apply at once. Rents Read more Read more For renters, the interest rate impact is more indirect. Some landlords may try to offset the impact of rate rises on their cash flow by raising rents over time, although there are constraints on how often and how much rent can be increased each year in most states. The RBA has also dismissed the idea that landlords pass their increased borrowing costs on to renters. Speaking on 9Now's The Pay Off podcast, RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter said what was really driving rents came down to supply and demand. "If you're an individual landlord, you own one property in one rental market, you might want to put the rent up when your interest rate goes up if you've got a mortgage," Dr Hunter said. "But you're competing with all the other properties that are available … and so, it's demand and supply; it's the local market that will equilibrate rent. "If rents are tracking up, it's usually because demand growth is stronger than supply growth." Ms Allen and Dr Oliver agree with this logic. Cotality's quarterly rental review found rents rose by 1.6 per cent nationally in the June quarter, driven by a severe lack of available stock across the country. The national dwelling vacancy rate sat at 1.6 per cent, unchanged from March and remaining below the five-year average of 1.8 per cent. "The main factor driving rents is the shortage of rental property," Dr Oliver says.

Savings Read more Read more There is one silver lining in the rate rise, for some. Savings accounts and term deposit interest rates usually rise after an RBA hike, making it more attractive to park your money. This is because, while the cash rate also affects borrowing costs for banks, it also sets the rate of return for their own deposits. Cash rate hikes improve their returns, which may be passed on to consumers through higher savings interest rates. Dr Oliver says while short-term deposit rates largely move in line with the cash rate, longer-term term deposit rates are also shaped by government bond yields and other borrowing costs. With today's RBA increase and bond yields already rising, he says savers are likely to benefit from higher returns. "The odds are, yes, we will see deposit rates continue to rise." Australian dollar Read more Read more Higher interest rates tend to strengthen the Australian dollar (AUD). And that's because it's more attractive for foreign investors to park their money in Australian interest-bearing assets (like savings accounts, term deposits, and government bonds) because they can get a higher rate of interest here. This increases demand for the AUD, making the currency more valuable. That generally means imported products can cost less in Australian-dollar terms and overseas travel becomes cheaper. But Ms Allen says the Australian dollar's value depends on far more than the RBA's cash rate decisions. "The Australian dollar is influenced by many things — global interest rates, commodity prices, China, investor sentiment and expectations about the Australian economy — so you can't say that a 25-basis-point rate hike will automatically result in a particular move in the dollar," she says. Dr Oliver agrees, noting that with the US Federal Reserve also tightening monetary policy, any upward pressure on the Australian dollar may be offset. "I suspect it probably just keeps the Aussie dollar around where it is," he says.

Car and personal loans Read more Read more Car loans and personal loans can be affected by increases in the cash rate. But it all comes down to what type of loan you have. Australians collectively borrowed around $4.7 billion in fixed-term personal loans for road vehicles in the three months to June 2026, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. These loans would not be affected by the cash rate until their fixed-rate period ends. For those on a variable rate, Dr Oliver says banks may not necessarily hike rates by the full 0.25 per cent, but "the odds are they'll probably go up over time as well".

Is this the last rate hike for the year?

We don't know.

The majority of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg expect the RBA to be done with hikes for the rest of the year.

Westpac, NAB and CBA are also in agreement.

In a weekly market update last Friday, Dr Oliver summed up the majority view.

"By the time it gets to the November meeting, there is likely to be more evidence of a cooling economy, falling home prices, a softer jobs market and rising recession risks, so we don't think a second hike let alone a third will be necessary," he wrote.

ANZ is the only major bank so far officially tipping a November rise as well, alongside HSBC and UBS.

Ms Allen says it all depends on the near-term movements in inflation data.

The RBA will deliver its next cash rate decision on Tuesday, November 3.

title: Breaking: RBA lifts rates to highest level in 15 years
text:
The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 15 years.

It has increased rates by 0.25 percentage points, which lifts the cash rate target to 4.6 per cent, up from 4.35 per cent.

It will be a blow to home owners with large mortgages. It is also the highest cash rate millions of households have faced since taking on a mortgage after 2011.

But individuals who have high-interest savings accounts will see their savings accruing more interest after today's decision, if their bank applies higher rates to their accounts.

The decision to lift rates was unanimous, with all nine members of the board voting in favour.

The desire to get inflation down

In recent weeks, senior RBA officials have been warning that they are losing patience with the time it is taking to drag inflation back down into the RBA's 2-3 per cent target range.

In July, headline inflation was running at an annual pace of 3.5 per cent and underlying (or "core") inflation was running at 3.6 per cent.

The RBA wants inflation sitting around 2.5 per cent on average, over the medium term.

But Australia is not alone in its struggle to get inflation down.

In recent weeks, the European Central Bank, US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and Reserve Bank of New Zealand have all lifted rates.

The latest fighting in the Middle East has also sent crude oil prices higher in recent weeks, which has pushed more inflation around the world via higher fuel prices.

The RBA's decision to lift interest rates today comes one day before the Bureau of Statistics releases its September quarter inflation data.

RBA prepared to lift rates again if necessary

In a statement, the RBA Board said it did not want high inflation to become embedded in Australia's economy.

It said since its last meeting, the conflict in the Middle East had broadened and global energy prices were now much higher.

Rate rise looking likely All four major banks and the bulk of money market traders believe the Reserve Bank will raise interest rates next week and governor Michele Bullock did nothing to dissuade them during a speech in Sydney.

It said AI-related demand was driving rapid growth in global prices for technology-related goods, and some Australian businesses were experiencing cost pressures and were either increasing prices or looking to do so.

It also said economic growth and inflation were both higher in Australia than had been expected, and interest rates needed to rise to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation back to target.

"The three increases in the cash rate target since the beginning of the year have tightened financial conditions and the economy appears to be slowing," it said.

"But inflation is still too high and the Board judged that, in light of recent developments, a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support a return of inflation to target in a reasonable period.

"The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed," it said.

title: How John Farnham pulled off one of music's greatest comebacks
text:
Forty years after its release, John Farnham's Whispering Jack remains one of the most remarkable stories in Australian music history.

The 1986 album spent 25 weeks at number one, produced enduring hits that remain part of our national conscience, and transformed John Farnham from a fading teen idol into one of the country's most beloved performers.

Whispering Jack topped the charts for 25 weeks. (Supplied)

Its centrepiece, You're The Voice, is bigger than a pop song: the unofficial anthem still inspires singalongs at pubs, stadiums and festival fields decades later.

None of it was supposed to happen.

By the mid-80s, Farnham's career was drifting. Record labels weren't interested. His attempts at chart success weren't connecting.

A stint fronting world-conquering Aussie rockers Little River Band didn't kickstart the resurgence he hoped for.

So, Whispering Jack wasn't the work of a music industry machine backing a sure thing. It was the result of the work of a small team of people convinced they saw something the rest of the industry had missed.

One last chance

John Farnham's first taste of fame came early.

As Johnny Farnham, he dominated Australian charts in the late 1960s and early 1970s, scoring a massive hit with Sadie (The Cleaning Lady), the best selling Australian single of the '60s.

But, as tastes changed, Farnham's commercial fortunes faded. He moved into musical theatre and TV, proving he remained an endearing entertainer, but not necessarily a recording artist to watch.

A reinvention was needed. Johnny became John. And while he had flashes of success, like cracking back into the Top 10 with a version of The Beatles's Help in 1980, the momentum didn't stick.

John Farnham later said he didn't feel like a good fit as the Little River Band frontman. (Supplied: Facebook)

His time with Little River Band proved valuable, particularly the exposure to large-scale touring in America, but didn't provide the breakthrough Farnham and his manager Glenn Wheatley, who died in 2022, were searching for.

By 1985, many in the industry believed Farnham's biggest successes were behind him. Wheatley never accepted that.

"We all knew what he had," Wheatley told News Corp in 2018. "He's one of the greatest singers of our time. We just had to find the right songs for him."

Finding songs wasn't too hard — there were plenty around. Finding someone willing to back the project was another story.

Neither record labels nor producers showed much interest. Eventually, Wheatley and Farnham decided to do it themselves.

"I had to find out whether I could get the money to make the album for a start," Farnham told the ABC's John Hall in 1987.

Wheatley's label became his record company and the gamble got bigger. The budget for the album was about $150,000.

Farnham and Wheatley worked together for decades. (AAP: Julian Smith)

Speaking to Jen Jewel Brown for the National Film and Sound Archive in 2014, Wheatley recalled: "I ended up having to do it on my label again. I had to mortgage my house to do it."

"I couldn't not do it; not to John," he recalled in Clark Forbes's 1989 book Whispering Jack.

"What the hell, I had nothing to lose either. I simply had to go for this."

We want to hear your fondest John Farnham memories. Share it with us here.

Building Whispering Jack

The team eventually settled on live sound engineer Ross Fraser as producer. He wasn't a known name, and it wasn't a conventional move.

Farnham was named Australian of the Year in 1987. (Supplied)

It turned out to be a masterstroke.

Together, Farnham, Fraser and Wheatley embarked on an exhaustive search for material.

"I must have listened to 2,000 songs, easy, from all over the world," Farnham told Hall.

"We sent telexes all over the world to all the publishers and record companies that we were looking for songs.

"We literally got two boxes, we put 'no' on one box and 'maybe' on the other box, and we just went through them all.

"I had to listen to the songs in their entirety because, being a budding songwriter myself, I understand how much work these people put into it. So, I had to at least give them that courtesy."

Even then, the work had barely begun.

The eventual album only contained 10 tracks, but every arrangement was meticulously worked over. A month of pre-production was followed by more than two months in the studio.

"We were in there for 18 hours a day, pumping away, and we really worked hard," Farnham told Hall.

You can still hear that commitment when you hit play on Whispering Jack 40 years on.

Its sound – synthesisers, drum machines and enormous production – is unmistakably rooted in the '80s. Yet somehow it doesn't feel trapped there.

The commitment in those performances — from Farnham and his band — and the strength of those songs prove this hard-won success was well deserved.

Finding You're The Voice

Whispering Jack was still missing something when a tape arrived from England.

Loading Instagram content

"The last song we found was You're The Voice," Wheatley told the National Film and Sound Archive.

A publisher insisted Farnham would love it.

"When I first heard it, my heart almost stopped," Farnham told the Toronto Star in 1987. "I felt like I'd discovered lost treasure."

According to the story that has since become part of Australian music folklore, label manager Doris Tyler heard the song first and wasn't especially convinced. But Ross Fraser was.

Driving to Farnham's house one afternoon, the producer reportedly played the cassette over and over. The more he listened, the more certain he was that the song had to be on the record.

It made the cut, but when it was released, it wasn't an easy sell. Wheatley and the team were dogged in chasing airplay before commercial radio fully embraced it.

Once they did, there was no stopping it.

The pay-off

You're The Voice became a phenomenon and its success propelled Whispering Jack to number one, where it remained for 25 weeks.

Follow-up singles Pressure Down, A Touch of Paradise and Reasons kept momentum rolling. The album became much bigger than anyone had dared imagine.

That mortgage Wheatley took out to fund the album was repaid many times over. Whispering Jack went on to become the highest-selling album in Australia by an Australian artist.

It also reached number six in the UK and topped the charts in Sweden. You're The Voice charted across Europe, an unusual feat for an Australian artist at the time.

John Farnham performs after sweeping the 1987 Countdown Awards. (Supplied: YouTube)

When Wheatley and Farnham heard the news that the album had reached number one, they were together in a car.

"I was saying, 'Do you realise John that we have a number one record?'" Wheatley recalled in Forbes's book Whispering Jack.

"I looked towards him at the traffic lights, and he had tears coming down his cheeks.

"He said, 'I can't believe this is happening'."

For Farnham, this wasn't just about commercial success, it was about vindication.

"I feel more credible now," he told the Toronto Star at the time.

"I'm really working hard.

"All my life things have come too easily to me. I put everything on the line this time. And now it feels as if I deserve it."

title: Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan presented with keys to the city
text:
Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan has been presented with the keys to the city after leading the team to a historic three AFL premierships in a row.

On Saturday, the Lions clawed back a 17-point deficit in the final four minutes of the grand final to defeat the Fremantle Dockers 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89).

The win was the team's third consecutive grand final victory, after defeating Sydney and Geelong in 2024 and 2025 respectively.

It marks the club's second three-peat, after it won the 2001, 2002 and 2003 premierships under coach Leigh Matthews.

Chris Fagan has led the Lions to three premiership wins. (Supplied)

Speaking at a Brisbane Lions fan day, Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner noted the team had been given the keys to the city after its first premiership in 2001. Today, he presented the keys to Fagan.

According to the Brisbane City Council, the keys to the city is a symbolic presentation that honours "an individual's or an organisation's outstanding achievement or contribution to our city".

"It may also be awarded to a Brisbane resident for an outstanding achievement in sport, community or humanitarian work."

Upon receiving the keys, Fagan asked: "The keys to the city, I don't know what that means — can I do anything?"

The Brisbane Lions were all smiles in front of the fans at Riverstage. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

Former Brisbane Lord Mayor Graham Quirk answered that question back in 2019. He said the key wouldn't get you very far.

"It's the highest accolade a city can provide to an individual or a group of individuals, but it doesn't get you anywhere in terms of physically opening doors," he said.

The presentation comes amid speculation over Fagan's future, as the coach has yet to confirm whether he will remain with the club for another year.

He is currently contracted until the end of the 2027 season.

Chris Fagan said he was unsure if he would remain as coach for another year. (ABC News)

Speaking to ABC News Breakfast on Monday, Fagan said he had "a few things to work out".

"Whether I've still got the absolute energy you need to do this job, because you do need a lot," he said.

"I've been doing it for 10 years now, and I just want to make sure that if I keep going, I can deliver to the players the amount of energy that I need to.

"It's a job that's got relentless responsibility and pressure around it."

title: US-China tariff cuts include emus, robots, whales and soccer balls
text:
Whales, surgical robots, emus and soccer balls will all face lower tariffs after China and the United States agreed to a $US60 billion ($85.5 billion) deal following US President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Both countries released lists of goods valued at $US30 billion each that are in line for a tariff cut, a move experts say is significant following last week's state visit in Washington.

There are 1,619 US goods entering China that will be eligible for lower tariffs including corn, hair and personal care products, timber and medical equipment like X-ray machines.

Live animals including whales for "pure-bred breeding", emus and dugongs are also listed, as are surgical robots.

Notably American soybeans, the US's largest single export to China, was not included.

The US listed 77 categories of Chinese goods, including fireworks, tableware, toys like dolls and puzzles, glass and wooden Christmas ornaments, soccer balls and household scales.

Rare earth minerals and technology linked to artificial intelligence were not included on either list and continue to face significant trade restrictions on both sides.

Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan visited Washington for a state visit last week. (Pool via Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

China's commerce ministry said in a statement that the agreement would help strengthen trade cooperation, with tariffs on more than 90 per cent of the products to be subject to "most-favoured nation" levels.

"Most-favoured nation" rates are the standard tariffs applied under World Trade Organization rules and are often in the single digits but can vary item to item.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a separate statement the product lists focused on "non-sensitive goods on each side that could benefit from more favourable tariff treatment".

Mr Greer said the deal could help secure better market access in China for US farmers and businesses, while American consumers would benefit from cheaper household goods.

American meat, wheat, dairy, vegetables and vegetable oil are all set to receive lower Chinese tariffs.

The lists could be adjusted later, both countries said, but were likely to be reviewed only on an annual basis.

Neither side detailed the specific reduction that items would face, nor a timeline to implement them.

ING Bank chief economist for Greater China Lynn Song said it could be the first step in boosting bilateral trade.

Deal a 'substantive step'

Monash University economics professor Shi Heling told the ABC, "it shows China and the US have taken a substantive step toward tariff reduction, or toward cooling the trade conflict".

He said while the deal was worth only a fraction of the total bilateral trade between the two countries, it had benefits for both China and the US.

The Chinese imports that have lower tariffs were household items and Christmas-related gifts, he said, which could help lower inflation heading into the festival shopping season.

For Xi, America is no longer the centre of China's strategy At the glittering high point of the White House state dinner, the hierarchy of the world's two great powers was laid bare.

"Politically speaking, there are US midterm elections in November, and American voters are extremely sensitive to prices. If inflation comes down before the midterms, that would really help Trump's administration," Professor Shi said.

"It's also good for China, because China imports agricultural products and medical products from the US, and if tariffs go up, ordinary Chinese people end up paying more."

He said US agricultural exports were much more important than the animals listed, which he believed were there "just to pad out the numbers, to make it look better".

He added that there was no guarantee this pact signalled a move toward a more substantial, long-term trade deal.

While the deal is small and does not involve Australia, director of the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney, James Laurenceson said the news would be welcomed in Canberra.

"For an open, trade-exposed economy like Australia, the fact that the world's two largest economies are better managing their own trade relationship is broadly a positive development," he told the ABC.

"There are limited exceptions to that, such as when our producers could sell goods to China while US producers were effectively locked out by high tariffs. Still, certainly in Canberra, I think the pause and modest tariffs reductions would be welcomed."

The agreement to cut tariffs was in addition to the deal struck to extend a trade truce through until January 2027.

ABC/wires

title: One last 'last' for Broncos legend Ali Brigginshaw in NRLW grand final
text:
Retiring Brisbane legend Ali Brigginshaw has one more NRLW match to play, but her competitive drive is just as strong as the day she took up playing rugby league at the age of 10.

The 38-year-old five-eighth will play against old foes the Sydney Roosters in the grand final with a team-first mentality, but also with the determination to get one over opposite number Jocelyn Kelleher the same way she did in the 20-8 preliminary final victory against Gold Coast.

Rugby sevens superstar Teagan Levi was wearing the number six and Brigginshaw had her measure.

"All the talk has been about her and I took it really personal[ly," she said.

"I said to the girls, 'I will do whatever I can to make sure I can shut her down.'

"I am just really proud. We trained extremely hard to get to this moment, but I am also proud of myself … 38 years old and I put myself in this position to be the best teammate and work my bum off whenever I play."

Teagan Levi and the Titans threatened the Broncos' premiership defence. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

When Brigginshaw won her fourth NRLW title last year, there were a couple of conversations about retiring with a premiership.

"People were saying it was a good ending, but I had all the belief in this team that we were going to get [to another grand final]," she said

"The hardest thing is getting there. You get there and you put yourself in the best position to compete and win it.

"It is a huge week and I am just excited to do it again because you never know when it is going to be your last … and this will be my last."

Brigginshaw calls herself, winger Julia Robinson and prop Chelsea Lenarduzzi "the OGs", being the three original Broncos from 2018 who are aiming for a fifth premiership with the club, while fullback Tamika Upton hopes to add a third Broncos crown to two won with Newcastle in 2022 and 2023.

Broncos into fifth NRLW grand final Brisbane will get the chance to send retiring club legend Ali Brigginshaw out a winner in the grand final after it overpowered Gold Coast 20-8 at Robina.

Only Michael Hancock and Kevin Walters have achieved the feat in Broncos history.

"We are the OGs. We are also good mates and they are part of the reason I love the Broncos," Brigginshaw said.

"Duzzi is passionate about everything she does and Robbo is the heart. The love they both have for the team and the jersey is what I love.

"We all just bleed for this jersey, and the best thing is that I see other people who want to do it and love the place as much as I do."

The Broncos lost eight players from last year's grand final side, but the new-look outfit, featuring superstar halfback Jesse Southwell, has bought in to the club's systems and culture.

"It is kind of frustrating how people forget how many we lost," Brigginshaw said.

"To win a premiership with them, then rebuild and get back here again … proves we have the right people here to give ourselves the best opportunity."

As a result of Brigginshaw's impending departure, everything at Red Hill has a "last" associated with it this year, whether it be her last game at home in a club match or her last preliminary final.

"It is just a bit of a joke around 'the last last'," she said.

"I have got there now, so let's have a crack."

title: Housing developer walks away from 1,900-home SA project
text:
"Hundreds" of homebuyers will not be left in limbo despite a major developer walking away from a new estate in Adelaide's north, the state's housing minister has insisted.

The Eyre development near Penfield, between Edinburgh and Andrews Farm, was announced in 2010, and includes plans for 1,900 homes on a 120-hectare site.

SA government agency Renewal SA said it had entered an agreement with developer AVJennings — since bought by AVID Property Group — to build the homes, and that "about 750" had been completed, along with sporting fields and a shopping centre.

But it said that AVID had made the decision to "conclude its activities" in the South Australian market, leaving the remainder of the project back in the hands of the SA government.

Acting Housing Minister Michael Brown said the state government would seek to partner with another developer to deliver the project, and that outstanding contracts would be honoured.

"There's a few hundred contracts," he said.

"AVJennings are absolutely adamant that they will be delivered … so those who have signed deals with AVJennings need not be concerned."

Mr Brown described AVID's move as "a commercial decision".

The ABC has contacted AVID for comment — but in a statement on its website, it said it had "agreed to transition the developer role at the Eyre community" to Renewal SA.

"The decision … is a strategic business decision reflecting AVID's focus on the Australian eastern seaboard," it said.

"While Renewal SA assumes responsibility for the future direction of the community, AVID remain committed to delivering in-progress and planned stages and amenities, including a park, streetscapes and blocks.

"If you hold a contract for a lot in Stage 17 or 18, your contract remains on foot and AVID remains your point of contact for all settlement-related matters."

Renewal SA says the project will "remain on track". (YouTube: Eyre Penfield)

Master Builders Association CEO Will Frogley told 891 ABC Adelaide it was "definitely disappointing" that the company had opted against further involvement in the project.

"The main thing that Master Builders would really like to see is stability in the market — there's a lot of turbulence at the moment," he said.

"Last year we built a record number of homes, so it is quite disappointing to see a brand that size, a national developer, moving away from South Australia."

Renewal SA said the project would "remain on track" and that the "transition would not affect existing purchasers".

It said AVID had committed to finishing "outstanding work on current stages, including landscaping and delivery of a reserve, while also working with existing buyers to finalise upcoming settlements required design approvals and ensure that all commitments to existing buyers are maintained".

It said that work was expected to be completed by mid-2027.

title: Soccer player with broken leg endures 70km car trip between hospitals
text:
The family of a soccer player injured in a game believe the decision to take him by ambulance to the closest regional hospital led to unnecessary pain and delayed surgery.

After waiting hours at Victor Harbor's South Coast District Hospital for an ambulance transfer, Harry Jones made the 70-kilometre dash to a metropolitan hospital in the back seat of a car.

Mr Jones, the captain of the senior men's team at the Southern Breakers Football Club, was injured during the last game of the season.

Harry Jones is the captain of the Southern Breakers senior men's team and started playing soccer with the club at the age of five. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

He caught his right boot in the goal net while trying to stop an opposition strike and landed awkwardly, breaking both bones in his lower left leg.

He later had surgery to insert a titanium rod into one of the broken bones.

Painful wait for surgery

Club trainer Peta Haldane, an experienced registered nurse and a nurse practitioner in training, administered first aid to Mr Jones while they waited for an ambulance.

Peta Haldane says it was obvious Harry Jones needed to be a transferred to a hospital equipped for complex orthopaedic surgery. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

She said it was obvious he had a complete fracture to both bones in his lower leg and should have been taken straight to Flinders Medical Centre (FMC) since the closest hospital, Victor Harbor's Southern Fleurieu Health Service, was not equipped to deal with the level of orthopaedic surgery he needed.

Harry Jones had surgery to insert a titanium rod in his tibia the following day. (Supplied: Anna Jones)

Instead, she believed SA Ambulance policies meant he had to be taken to the nearest hospital.

His fiancee, Victoria Briggs said Mr Jones was in "excruciating pain" as he was X-rayed. He then waited for a transfer to FMC.

She said staff advised them they could be waiting another four to five hours for an ambulance and there was "no guarantee" he would be transferred that day.

According to Ms Briggs, a staff member told them "if it was them" they would use a private car to move him.

She took this advice and transferred Mr Jones herself, with the help of his mother, so he could undergo surgery that same day as his leg was continuing to swell.

Despite their efforts, Mr Jones still had to wait until the next day for surgery.

Tori Briggs transported Harry Jones to the Flinders Medical Centre in the back seat of this car with the help of his mother. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Call for change

Ms Briggs and Ms Haldane have urged the health minister to consider Mr Jones's experience and the delays and pain he experienced.

They have also raised concern for others on the Fleurieu needing orthopaedic surgery, questioning if they could be sent straight to a metropolitan hospital.

Do you know more? Contact Caroline Horn on horn.caroline@abc.net.au

Ms Briggs stressed they had no issues with the care he had received.

"The paramedics were fabulous. All the hospital staff have been wonderful … but something needs to change," she said.

Gordon Scott says most people would have made the same decision to drive a loved one themselves. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Mr Jones's coach, former police officer Gordon Scott, backed Ms Briggs and Ms Haldane's call for a review.

He said someone undertaking a car transfer themselves for an injured loved one could emotionally compromise their driving.

"If you're being told there's no patient transport available to transport your loved one for several hours and a better option is to take them in your private car then you're probably going to take that option," he said.

Destination policy

A spokesperson from SA Ambulance said the ambulance crew had made the decision to take Mr Jones to the Victor Harbor hospital to "ensure the patient would receive the quickest medical care and quick access to appropriate pain relief options".

"The SA Health ambulance destination policy looks at a range of considerations, one of which is transport to an 'appropriate and geographically closest' hospital, as well as other considerations such as the patient's immediate health care needs, demand on individual hospitals etc," they said in a statement.

"These decisions are made by appropriate healthcare professionals, depending on the patient's individual needs."

title: A would-be surrogate gave us a gift. It wasn't the one we were expecting
text:
I started sharing my failures in fertility five years ago.

Mostly because I have a big mouth. And I couldn't dodge the constant question: "Do you have kids?" Everyone asks it. Colleagues, acquaintances, that person I bumped into on the way to the bin.

I expected sharing my miscarriages and failed IVF transfers to bring in a barrage of advice: "Sashi, have you tried [insert doctor, product, test, treatment or magic spell]?"

It was so well-intentioned that I fast learnt to politely nod while internally howling into a canyon.

I also expected strangers to short-circuit in response to my breaking of the social contract to only share good news.

Once, after hearing of my miscarriages, a woman put her hands on my stomach and said, "I do declare your womb will bear, by the will of God."

I politely nodded so the barbecue could continue. Unfortunately, whichever god she contacted was busy.

What I never expected was the outpouring of support, and to hear from so many in the same situation.

What I also didn't expect was a stranger to volunteer as a surrogate.

Last spring, I shared the stranger's message with my husband, Charlie. After firmly deciding to take a break from IVF, I had researched other options with the zeal of an Olympic sprinter hurtling towards the finish line.

The waters of international adoption and commercial surrogacy appeared murky and expensive. Now, here was a surrogate in our own city. Someone who seemed far too altruistic for the cynical world shouted about on the nightly news.

Finding out her fertility struggles weren't about her body being unable to carry a child gave Sashi a sense of freedom she had not felt in a long time. (Supplied: Sashi Perera)

Charlie said: "That's got to be a weirdo, love," and I said: "Almost definitely, but it's worth a phone call."

That call led to meeting a kind and lovely human at a cafe a few months later. She was married with two kids and felt compelled by our story to contact me. There are good people doing good things constantly, they're just not featured in the news too often.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

I looked into the state of Victoria's surrogacy process, which requires counselling, legal advice and medical approvals. Even with two law degrees, it was a lot to decipher.

We decided to walk the path lined with endless paperwork. The first step was to get approval from my IVF clinic. I thought that would be the easiest one. I didn't expect the answer I got.

"You can do this," they said over the phone, "but it's unlikely to make a difference in your case."

It was the first time I was told the problem likely wasn't my body, it was the embryos. For whatever reason the tests couldn't pinpoint, they weren't keepers.

I'd spent so long feeling guilty. It was why I'd researched every other path, to the exasperation of Charlie, who said we'd be fine without kids.

I'd taken every pill and potion available, consulted with a UK-based naturopath I've never seen or met, used a hormone tracking device to monitor my daily pee, and watched what I ate, drank and how I slept.

I thought that if I did enough, I could shake the guilt that screamed it was my defective body's fault that we couldn't grow a family.

And now, I'd found a whole other, clearly functioning body. And that still wasn't enough?!

I should've felt fury but all I felt was relief.

My shoulders dropped from the level of my ears. I didn't even know they were up there. Or how long they'd been like that for.

Years ago, I tried wakeboarding for the first time. I was really struggling to stay on the board and was distracted by the thought that waterboarding was a far more sensible term for boarding on the water — why did we use that term for a terrible form of torture instead?

My friend shouted from the boat, you're fighting with the rope for control instead of letting it guide you, you've got to relax your hold.

I've been told to relax my whole life and would you believe, it's never helped me to relax. But the moment I slackened my hold on the rope that tethered me to the boat, I flew over the water on a board.

I thought about that moment after my call with the IVF clinic.

Being told to relax her whole life never helped Sashi relax, except that one time wakeboarding. Letting go of her need to solve infertility felt a little like that. (Supplied: Sashi Perera)

For the first time, I believed that it was not my fault and there was nothing more I could do. I threw every pill and test into the bin along with the hormone monitoring device. I fished that last one back out because it was quite expensive and might come in handy for menopause.

With no finish line for me to sprint towards, I discovered the ability to relax my hold and enjoy whatever's ahead, without trying to control it.

I'm now on the biggest tour of my comedy career with Charlie. The surrogate gave us a gift, just not in the way we expected.

title: Crossland expected to miss grand final with guilty plea over Cleary tackle
text:
Newcastle Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland will plead guilty at the judiciary over the tackle that left Nathan Cleary with a compound fracture.

Crossland was sent off for the hip-drop tackle in the 36th minute of Newcastle's preliminary final win over Penrith on Sunday and the match review committee sent him straight to the judiciary with a dangerous contact charge.

A hearing is set for 6pm AEST tonight to decide the punishment, with Crossland's plea all but guaranteeing he will miss Sunday's grand final, barring an 11th-hour miracle.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

Dragons forward Ryan Couchman was referred straight to the judiciary in round three for a hip drop that ended the season of Parramatta's J'Maine Hopgood.

Couchman pleaded guilty and was suspended for four games after being sin-binned for the tackle that left Hopgood with a torn ACL.

"Whilst the panel accepted that this did not incorporate any element of intention or recklessness, it took the view that the player's level of culpability was significant, a factor reflected in the serious injury sustained by the ball carrier," judiciary chair Geoff Bellew said during a 90-minute hearing.

Crossland has apologised to Cleary, who urged people to stop abusing the Knights number nine online.

"It was a complete accident, and he doesn't deserve the unwarranted hate. He reached out to apologise, and I have nothing but respect for him," Cleary posted on social media after surgery on his broken left leg.

Phoenix Crossland was sent off as Nathan Cleary left on a medicab. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"He's a competitor, and our game is made up of split-second moments that sometimes lead to unfortunate circumstances.

"Comments like this are so unfair. Spread love, not hate."

Newcastle football director Chris James on Monday described it as "a horrible accident at speed under fatigue".

"Phoenix Crossland has made more tackles in the NRL than any other player and he got one wrong," he told ABC Sport.

"He got one wrong and it was a horrible injury for Nathan, but that's not Phoenix's go. If you've ever met Phoenix Crossland, he's one of the great men of rugby league.

"Horrible for Nathan, the thoughts of our club go out to Nathan.

"He'll go down as one of the greats of the game and we hope he has a speedy recovery, but we'll also wrap our arms around Phoenix and make sure we look after him this week too."

title: After a one-night stand, this comedian was told he’d be a dad. But not all was as it seemed
text:
Comedian Simon Taylor got sick of being asked why he doesn’t have a podcast, so made a sitcom about podcasters.

Comedian Simon Taylor received a Facebook message after a casual encounter. It changed his life – just not in the way he imagined.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Among the people inadvertently promoting Simon Taylor’s new sitcom The Sonny Disposition – a satire about the chaotic, ego-driven world of podcasting – are Kyle Sandilands, Karl Stefanovic and Anthony Albanese. “The timing is perfect,” says the comedian, who created the series with Josh Samuels. “Every day, someone in my team is messaging me going, ‘Kyle Sandilands just started a podcast! Karl’s in the news for an episode about right-wing extremists!’ And then Albo got himself in trouble [over the so-called melon-gate affair].” But the idea for The Sonny Disposition occurred well before these headline-grabbing incidents. “It actually came from me not wanting to do a podcast,” says the 38-year-old, who was hired as a writer for The Tonight Show with Jay Leno at 24 before becoming the first Australian stand-up to perform on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. “Everyone’s like, ‘You’re a comedian; where’s your podcast?’ But I’m so sick of them. There are so many already, and I don’t know what I’d be offering that’s different. So I’m offering this instead – a sitcom about podcasters.” What fascinates Taylor is the medium’s “Wild West” aspect, and the performative authenticity of many hosts. “As a journalist, you have to follow ethical guidelines,” he says. “But as a podcaster, you can reach an audience without any of those pesky ethics. You get to be the CEO as well as the face of the show. You’re a gunslinger; you’ll do anything to beat the other guy’s ratings and win over the algorithm.”

Advertisement

Worst habit? Drinking coffee after 9pm. I always feel like I need to get a bit more work done before bed so I’ll have a coffee, work until 1am and then sleep better knowing I’ve ticked off a few things. It’s a terrible health habit but my mum’s side of the family is Italian, and my grandparents would always have coffee after dinner, so maybe I have enough Italian DNA to handle it. Greatest fear? I have nightmares about my wife ghosting me. I’ll wake up and go, “You left me again, you blocked me.” But my wife and I have a good rule. We don’t say, “You did this in my dreams”; I’ll say, “Dream Lucy did this”, and she’ll say, “Dream Simon did this.” If I were to psychoanalyse myself, I’d guess it’s about losing what makes me happiest: being at home with my family. Taylor (centre) with the cast of The Sonny Disposition. The line that stayed with you? There’s variations of this line going around but my friend, Philip Escoffey, a magician from the UK, distilled it into a nice quote: “Luck gets you through the door but hard work determines how long you stay there.” In a career like this, you never know when you’ll get a break. I’ve had lucky moments, but to stay in the game I have to keep writing jokes so I’m always ready. I know people who make a living from social media, but I’m not jealous of them because they’re constantly posting and checking their numbers, even when they’re talking to their friends. If I did that, it would change my relationship with my family. I just want to get home, put my phone on “do not disturb” and engage with my kids.

Advertisement

Biggest regret? Not embracing the comedy community earlier. When I started, I thought I was a lone wolf. It took me 10 years to realise that this is a team sport in many ways. We’re a collective of comedians who look after each other. Related Article Take 7 How Aja Monet traded poetry slams for Grammy nods Tell us about your turning point … I wrote a book about this. In my 20s, I had a one-night stand – and then I was told I was going to be a dad. I got a Facebook message, then a phone call. I was 27, very career-focused and on the road a lot. That’s when the world changed for me. I was really emotional; I was excited but also worried because I didn’t really know the woman. Then I was told, “No, it might be another guy.” So it was nine months of me waiting to see whether it was me or this other guy. When I did the test, I found out I wasn’t the dad. But it was a turning point for me in the dating world because it made me realise that I wanted to be a father. Until then, I felt lacking, like there was something missing. This allowed me to be upfront and say, “I want marriage and kids.”

title: The hidden cost of downsizing: How your home’s sale can hit your pension

MoneySuper & retirementPension Opinion The hidden cost of downsizing: How your home’s sale can hit your pension Rachel Lane Money contributor September 29, 2026 — 3:00pm

September 29, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Downsizing can free up equity to invest or spend. But for retirees receiving the age pension that can be a problem as you may be converting an exempt asset into an assessable one. New data from over-50s developer GemLife shows that, of 1474 purchasers across 12 communities, the average equity release was $254,098 when downsizing into a land lease community. Downsizing your home can mean downsizing your pension. A Stockland land lease community. That $254,000 can boost your savings, buy a new car, caravan or boat or help out the kids but it can also reduce your pension and other benefits. For pensioners, the magic numbers are $333,000 if you’re single and $499,000 for couples. These are the asset test thresholds. Once your assessable assets exceed the threshold, your pension reduces by $3 a fortnight for every $1000 above the threshold.

Advertisement

Put simply you lose $7800 per year of pension for every $100,000 of assets over the threshold. Related Article Opinion

Aged care The alarming reason one in three seniors are giving up aged care Rachel Lane Money contributor So what does releasing $254,000 actually mean? Well, it depends on what you start with. A single person starting with $50,000 in assets would have $304,000. They would be below the $333,000 threshold, so there would be no reduction under the assets test. If they started with $250,000, their assets would rise to $504,000, which is $171,000 over the threshold, their pension would be reduced by $513 a fortnight, or $13,338 a year.

Advertisement

And if they started with $500,000 they would have $754,000 after they downsize, that’s over the cut-off of $745,750, so their pension would be lost. Couples can have more. A couple starting with $200,000 would have $454,000 after they move, and still be below the $499,000 assets threshold. The question isn’t just how much equity can you unlock: it’s how much retirement income you will have left once you do. If they started with $500,000 they would have $754,000 which is $255,000 above the threshold, reducing their pension by about $765 a fortnight, or $19,890 a year, under the assets test. And if they start with $867,000 or more the move would push them above the $1.121 million cut-off and their pension would be lost.

Advertisement

These examples are deliberately looking only at the assets test. How you invest or spend matters. If you invest it, the income can help offset any pension reduction, but the deemed income will be used to calculate your pension under the income test. Related Article Ask an expert ‘Shock and disbelief’: The pitfalls of buying property with your children If you spend it on a boat, car or caravan, those assets still count under the assets test but only at market value. It’s important to understand that your pension will be paid based on whichever test, income or assets, produces the lowest pension. Downsizing your home can mean downsizing your pension, that doesn’t automatically make it a bad decision. You need to understand how much equity you will release, what you will do with it and how it will affect your pension and other benefits. In a land lease community getting at least some pension can take on extra importance because the site fees qualify as rent for rent assistance, potentially adding up to $5819 a year (single) or $5486 (couple) on top of your pension.

The question isn’t just how much equity can you unlock: it’s how much retirement income you will have left once you do. title: RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6 per cent in 15-year high, open to further hikes
text:
Advertisement

The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to a 15-year high to combat stubborn inflation and has not ruled out further hikes despite rising unemployment, falling house prices and sluggish economic growth. The bank’s monetary policy board decided unanimously to raise its benchmark cash rate by 0.25 of a percentage point to 4.6 per cent on Tuesday, adding more than $90 a month to repayments on a typical $600,000 mortgage with 25 years remaining. RBA governor Michele Bullock. Louie Douvis The increase means Australia now has one of the highest official interest rates set by a central bank among western economies, surpassing the US (where official rates are 4 per cent) and UK (3.75 per cent). In a statement, the RBA board left the door open for additional interest rate increases, saying it will “continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed”.

Advertisement

The board said previously flagged “upside risks” to inflation were now materialising, citing the fallout from war in the Middle East, the AI boom and prices surges across the economy. “There have been further disruptions to global oil supply and recent data suggest that growth and inflation in Australia have been higher than expected,” the board said. “Higher fuel prices have partially been passed through to prices of other goods and services. This inflation impulse is in addition to the effect of capacity pressures in the economy.” The board acknowledged the housing downturn, noting that “weak productivity growth continues to constrain potential growth and there are uncertainties about the economic effects of the downturn in the housing market”.

Advertisement

The last time Australia’s cash rate was above 4.5 per cent was October 2011. However, the amount of outstanding mortgage debt has more than doubled since then. The total value of residential mortgages in 2011 was $1.05 trillion, but that has since climbed to $2.51 trillion, according the Australian Prudential Regulatory Authority. The RBA has now lifted interest rates by 1 percentage point over four separate increases this year in a bid to reduce inflation. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6 per cent in 15-year high; OpenAI apologises for Medicare data breach Price pressures have been stoked by elevated fuel prices caused by the Middle East conflict, which has dragged on since February and continues to disrupt global oil supplies. Average petrol prices in Australia have risen well above the $2-a-litre mark in the past month, putting pressure on the Albanese government to revive the fuel excise cuts that subsidised the cost for four months from April through July this year, and spurring other price rises as firms pass on this cost. The RBA’s decision also follows a volatile period of international bond markets as global interest rates climb to two decade highs amid concerns about higher inflation and geopolitical risk.

Advertisement

Australia’s inflation rate is currently 3.5 per cent and has been above the RBA’s target band of 2 to 3 per cent for much of the past five years. Reserve Bank officials have repeatedly expressed concern that expectations of elevated inflation have becoming more entrenched among business and consumers. Last month the unemployment rate reached 4.6 per cent, the highest rate in nearly five years, but the deterioration in the labour market was not enough to deter the RBA from lifting interest rates. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock warned last week the jobless rate may need to rise as high as 5 per cent to ease pressure on inflation. Higher interest rates will hit a housing market already weakened by higher borrowing costs and federal tax changes. Figures released in early September by property analytics firm Cotality showed house values have fallen for five consecutive months. The Australian stock market was down very slightly after the Reserve Bank of Australia met expectations and raised the cash rate to 4.6 per cent, up 25 basis points, on Tuesday afternoon.

Advertisement

The ASX 200 index had been trading at 8690, up about 0.11 per cent for the day, at 2.20pm AEST. At 2.32pm, just after the rates call, the index was at 8675, down 0.04 per cent. The central bank’s decision had been widely expected among market watchers and investors. Ahead of the decision, AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said he expected the bank to continue warning of further rate hikes, but that the tone may shift later in the year. “After more than five years of inflation being above target, threatening RBA credibility, it does not have the luxury of continuing to ‘wait and assess’,” he said. “By the time it gets to the November meeting, there is likely to be more evidence of a cooling economy, falling home prices, a softer jobs market and rising recession risks – so we don’t think a second hike let alone a third will be necessary.”

Advertisement

Oliver said rate hikes and higher petrol prices have raised the additional monthly costs for an average household by $530 a month since January for those with a mortgage and petrol car, which he said was “quite a hit”. The economy grew by 2.1 per cent last financial year, but gross domestic product per person rose by a more subdued 0.7 per cent. The Reserve Bank is forecasting growth the slow to 1.5 per cent in the year to June 2027. Inflation peaked at nearly 8 per cent at the end of 2022 but then fell back to the RBA’s 2–3 per cent target range for a period in 2024 and 2025. However, it picked up in the second half of 2025 and has remained above the target since. Bullock and other RBA officials have said repeatedly the bank is focused on getting inflation back into the 2-3 per cent band. title: Accelerate grabs full control of Pilbara manganese play

Accelerate Resources has grabbed full control of its Woodie Woodie North manganese project 260 kilometres east of Port Hedland in WA’s East Pilbara region in a savvy move that clears the decks of all legacy payments and royalties ahead of a significant drilling campaign planned for next month. The company has executed two binding, share-only agreements that deliver 100 per cent of the 432-square-kilometre tenure. The deals simplify a previously complex ownership structure and remove any future milestone payments, which could otherwise have potentially cost the company up to $2 million in cash and 20 million shares. Outcropping manganese at Accelerate Resources’ Woodie Woodie North project, just 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine in the Pilbara. In the first transaction, Accelerate will acquire full title to two key exploration licences by issuing 25 million shares to subsidiaries of First Development Resources. The shares will be subject to a 12-month voluntary escrow period. Previously, the company held only the manganese and iron ore rights over the tenements under a 2021 option. The deal now gives it outright ownership and extinguishes all remaining claims, including milestone payments and royalties.

Advertisement

‘All manganese we discover and develop at Woodie Woodie North will now belong solely to Accelerate shareholders.’ Accelerate Resources chief executive officer and managing director Luke Meter A second transaction involves Accelerate issuing 30 million shares to a group of seven unrelated vendors to terminate all legacy agreements across the wider project. The move scrubs all future milestone payments, deferred consideration, royalties and reversionary rights tied to resource definition and development. The company says the two scrip-based deals mean no cash will leave its coffers for the acquisitions, leaving it well-funded for its upcoming exploration push. Key to the consolidation is that Accelerate now stands to capture 100 per cent of the upside from any future discovery, resource upgrade or development at Woodie Woodie North. Management says the simplified structure will also better support any potential funding, offtake or partnering discussions down the track. Accelerate Resources chief executive officer and managing director Luke Meter said: “This is a decisive simplification of the Woodie Woodie North ownership structure. On Completion, we will own the Area 42 corridor outright and every remaining milestone payment across the project will be extinguished, with no cash leaving the Company. From that point, all manganese we discover and develop at WWN will belong solely to Accelerate shareholders.”

Advertisement

The Woodie Woodie North project sits 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine. The company has already carved out a maiden inferred mineral resource of 1.2 million tonnes grading 19.1 per cent manganese, alongside an exploration target of between 5.3 and 10.7 million tonnes at grades of 10 to 19 per cent manganese. Being on the doorstep of a major, multi-decade mining operation is an enviable position for any explorer. Perhaps more importantly though, the at-surface geology doesn’t respect tenement boundaries, with Accelerate saying it appears to be sitting on a significant extension of the same mineralised system that has made its neighbour a globally significant producer. With the ownership structure now cleaned up, the company is turning its focus to the drill bit. Scheduled for October, maiden drilling at the project’s Gingarrigan prospect follows recent mapping that identified more than 200 manganese outcrops across it and the nearby El Largo area, outlining a combined manganese footprint of almost 10 hectares. Rock chip sampling from the outcrops returned high-grade results of up to an impressive 59.4 per cent manganese. The upcoming 3000-metre reverse-circulation program will test the continuity of the surface mineralisation at depth and along strike, with management eyeing the potential to add a second resource area to the project.

Additionally, rock chip sampling from the company’s newly defined Rancor and Wampa prospects has returned grades as high as 58.4 per cent manganese, with a slew of other impressive hits including 57.6 per cent and 55.6 per cent manganese. For context, Australia’s two major operating mines at Woodie Woodie and Groote Eylandt run resource grades of 45.5per cent and 43.6 per cent manganese, respectively. The outcropping grades look bang on for direct-shipping ore (DSO). DSO is the holy grail for bulk commodity miners, meaning the ore is high-grade enough to be dug up and shipped directly to customers with minimal processing, dramatically slashing both capital and operating costs. Accelerate’s focus on manganese is part of a dual-pronged strategy, which also includes the Balagundi gold project near Kalgoorlie. In a nod to its two key commodities, the company is planning to rebrand as “Mango Metals”, a combination of the words manganese and gold. For now, however, all eyes are on the manganese. Having tidied up its ownership and removed the burden of legacy payments, Accelerate has a clear run at its Pilbara project. If the upcoming drilling at Gingarrigan can convert those high-grade surface rocks into a significant discovery, taking full control of the project will look like a very shrewd piece of business indeed. title: How Europe’s abandoned villages are being transformed
text:
Advertisement

InspirationEurope How Europe’s abandoned villages are being transformed Chrissie McClatchie Updated September 29, 2026 — 2:14pm ,first published September 29, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Tuscan resort of Castelfalfi is at maximum capacity for its annual Spring Festival in late March – quite literally; it’s a sell-out. In December, 30,000 people came for its Christmas market, so management made the smart decision to ticket this weekend event, while keeping it free for locals. Even so, it still seems like every family in the Pisa-Siena-Florence triangle is making an appearance at some point over the two-day program, if the line of parked cars lining every access road to the hilltop village is anything to go by. Visitors descend on Castelfalfi for the annual spring festival in late March. As hotel guests, my 10-year-old daughter, Lottie, and I need only to flash our room key and we’re ushered straight past the security fence, where an explosion of music from competing loudspeakers awaits. Some stallholders – selling everything from potted flowers to truffle paste and lots of pretty handmade jewellery (including a lemon pendant necklace blown from Murano glass that’s calling my name) – look increasingly fatigued by the mash-up of Britney Spears and ABBA blasting through the air from different directions.

Advertisement

I, however, am completely swept up in the buzz, singing along while sipping a Paloma spritz poured from one of the food trucks. In classic pre-teen fashion, Lottie – deep in her own culinary heaven thanks to a bombolone (doughnut) filled with Kinder chocolate – keeps her distance from her ever-embarrassing mother. Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. Via Castelfalfi Castello and Via Castelfalfi haven’t always been so lively. In fact, for most of the late 20th century, the two streets that made up this borgo were silent. In a copy and paste of thousands of medieval settlements across Italy, the hillcrest village had emptied; the last of its residents lured to the big smoke and the opportunities it offered in the 1950s. Resort life in the countryside ... Castelfalfi’s pool. Junior suite at Castelfalfi … the property has secured two Michelin Keys and a Forbes five-star rating. The buttercream-toned huddle of stone buildings overlooking the Valdera – one of Tuscany’s lesser-known patches, yet only 45 minutes from both Pisa and San Gimignano – stood tall but forgotten, mementos of a bygone era when these valleys hummed with rural life.

Advertisement

Nearly two decades ago, German tourism group TUI acquired the entire village and its surrounding estate and took the first steps in transforming it into a high-end eco-resort. In 2021, it was sold to Indian-Indonesian billionaire Sri Prakash Lohia. The new owner has raised the bar. Among Castelfalfi’s current accolades are two Michelin Keys and a Forbes Travel Guide five-star rating, no doubt hooked on features such as a signature suite designed by Stefano Ricci inside the village’s 14th-century castle. En suite in the Stefano Ricci-designed La Rocca suite. Across the estate’s 1090 hectares, guests can book on-site activities ranging from truffle hunting and wine tasting to pizza making, lake fishing, e-bike touring and a night jeep safari. A sleeping beauty awakened, Castelfalfi’s fairytale is part of a growing hospitality trend that’s breathing new life into Europe’s abandoned hamlets and villages.

Advertisement

Many of these villages-turned-hotels fall under the concept of albergo diffuso, Italian for scattered hotels. The term is a nod to the typical character of these properties: rooms spread across multiple buildings in a village, with guests navigating cobblestone streets and covered alleyways instead of internal staircases and lifts to access communal areas such as breakfast rooms, reception desks and restaurants. Castelfalfi’s dining options include a sweet gelateria and a delicatessen straining under the weight of different styles of pecorino cheese, alongside a cosy pizzeria tucked along its main streets. Meals are accompanied by the estate’s olive oils (the rosemary-infused variety paired with freshly baked focaccia is a meal in itself), and attentive waitstaff top up my glass with elegant house wines. One of several dining options within the restored historical Castelfalfi Borgo village complex. Not all reborn villages come with Castelfalfi’s luxury trimmings – or price tag. Some of the most memorable reveal themselves only after dedicated internet sleuthing. That’s how another Italian spot, Colletta di Castelbianco, appeared on my radar more than a decade ago. Near the French border in Liguria, the village was severely damaged in an 1887 earthquake. Inhabitants started to trickle away, and by the 1970s, the population was a mere five people. In the 1980s, a group of local entrepreneurs banded together to revitalise it, emphasising original materials and techniques in the rebuild. Ahead of its time – and certainly pre the global pandemic remote work boom – the project was imagined as a “teleworking” community, although now it has a definite out-of-office vibe.

Advertisement

Colletta di Castelbianco was planned as a “teleworking” community before the COVID remote work boom. The hamlet appears glued among thick vegetation to the slopes of the unspoilt Pennavaira valley, about 20 minutes inland from the seaside resort of Albenga. Its silhouette resembles a cluster of Greek Island homes, only with flat-roofed buildings fashioned from slate grey stones rather than whitewashed walls. There’s nothing but nature’s greens for company, which I admire while floating in a lap pool built into the terraced landscape. A casual, vine-covered bar and bistro beckons for late afternoon aperitivo that drifts into dinner. The preserved medieval stone architecture of Colletta di Castelbianco. Tucked up in the northern reaches of France’s vine-speckled Languedoc region, Village Castigno is a scattered hotel in the village of Assignan that’s long been on my travel wish-list, too. While never abandoned, Assignan’s population had dwindled to less than 200, and the village’s demographics were steadily ageing when Belgian couple Marc and Tine Verstraete purchased and restored the nearby 12th-century chateau Castigno in 2007.

Advertisement

Late last year, when road-tripping across France’s Mediterranean arc with my sister and younger daughter, I thought I’d stumbled upon a savvy hack. Why pay €300-plus for a family room at the hotel when I could book a privately owned house in the village – with an “excellent 9.0 rating” on booking.com – for €77, instead? With the savings, I reasoned, we could splash out on dinner at Castigno’s acclaimed Thai restaurant, inside a spacious village house, and return as external guests for breakfast – coming out more or less even. Apart from where we slept, our stay would revolve around Castigno’s facilities. Check-in with our friendly host is smooth and our cottage home, called La Maison De Blanche Neige (Snow White’s House) for the evening is, on first impressions, cute if not a little musty. We don’t linger, keen to reach Chateau Castigno’s tasting room before it closes for the day at 5pm. Castigno’s acclaimed Thai restaurant, Le Thai de Castigno. Inside an impressive cork-wrapped structure shaped like a wine bottle when viewed from above, our cellar host shares the backstory: when the Verstraetes acquired the chateau and the surrounding vineyards, their intention was simply to make wines to enjoy with friends in their new home. Opportunity soon came knocking. Not only did they snap up 150 hectares of land surrounding the chateau, but also derelict properties in the village at their doorstep. Today, guests lodge in one of 21 rooms in apartments and standalone houses, temporary neighbours alongside Assignan’s permanent population of 160.

Advertisement

Related Article Travel tips The world’s 10 most charming villages (plus five in Australia) As we swill and swirl the vineyard’s fresh, juicy sparkling rosé, I mention where we’re staying. Our host nearly spits out his wine: it turns out that Snow White’s House doubles as a “love room”, available for short-stay rendezvous of the “romantic” kind – explaining the hooks on the ceiling in the main bedroom. We dissolve into laughter, the lesson swiftly learnt to book within the official scattered hotels themselves. Yet, our adventure makes for a great story when we return, and is one additional tale to add to the countless layers of history these old stone villages across the continent hold. THE DETAILS STAY

Castelfalfi (castelfalfi.com) doubles from €810, including breakfast; Colletta di Castelbianco (colletta.it) apartments from €88, based on double occupancy, direct bookings; Village Castigno (villagecastigno.com) doubles from €146 (open April to mid-December).
