OpenAI has apologised to Australians after revealing its AI model took credentials and internal files from a Medicare portal and attempted to breach NSW and Victorian government systems. In a blog post on Tuesday, titled “How we will do better for Australia”, the company said an experimental model found a way into Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service in June. Once inside, it “ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, and wrote files”. The model also reviewed the service’s technical system information and source code. Sam Altman’s OpenAI has published fresh details on how its agents breached a Medicare website. Bloomberg “We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said. “We also should have handled our response better.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday he had a “direct but constructive discussion” with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman last week. On Monday, he was briefed in Canberra on the work of the government’s taskforce investigating the incident.

Advertisement

“OpenAI have been very constructive and open in engaging in that process, and I welcome that,” Albanese said. He said Anthropic had also engaged constructively. OpenAI detailed how the hacks unfolded and pledged to make changes. In the lengthy post, it said it has now blocked live internet access in its research environments, and has paused training and evaluation involving tool use for its most capable models. It will set up a taskforce including independent Australian experts to recommend how AI developers and governments should detect and disclose incidents, with a report due by the end of the year. It also offered Australian governments and industry credits from its $1 billion Daybreak cyber defence fund. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks at the UN last week. Dominic Lorrimer The breach was prompted when the model was set a research task: to find government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities. When it could not find the figures, it took actions OpenAI “had not authorised it to take”, the company said.

Advertisement

OpenAI named three other agencies whose systems its models reached. At the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, a model used a public crime mapping tool that returned application configuration, operational jobs and logs. At the Victorian Department of Health, agents found an exposed access key and used it to query the Victorian Agency for Health Information’s reporting system. Attempts to bypass access controls failed at the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. OpenAI said no individual crime, medical or survey records were accessed in any of the incidents. Related Article Updated

AI OpenAI halts powerful new AI model over fears it could go rogue The company said it found the activity in mid-August, during a review prompted by a July breach at AI platform Hugging Face. It notified Services Australia and the Victorian Department of Health on September 10, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics on September 18 and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare on September 24. OpenAI said the institute’s case “did not meet our disclosure thresholds” because the access seemed consistent with public access. “We should have shared preliminary findings sooner and kept Australian agencies updated as more facts emerged,” it said.

Advertisement

Albanese said the incidents showed the risks of the technology, alongside its benefits for productivity, health and research. “There are risks, and we’ve seen those risks exposed not just in what occurred in Australia, but the revelation that has occurred in the United States and other countries as well,” he said on Tuesday. OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will fly in from the US to appear before parliament’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney on October 6, as this masthead reported on Monday. Anthropic will appear before the same committee that day. Neither company will appear at Thursday’s hearing of a separate Senate inquiry into AI and data centres. “We know we have a lot of work ahead of us to rebuild trust,” OpenAI said. title: Japan could redraw the global oil map
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsOil Opinion Japan could redraw the global oil map

Javier Blas September 29, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Among the world’s top fuel-consuming nations, Japan is the most energy insecure. Its import-dependency ratios are scary: It buys overseas 99.9 per cent of the oil it needs; 99.7 per cent of the coal; and 97.8 per cent of the natural gas. So Tokyo springs into action after every major energy shock to reassess its supply sources, making it a bellwether of global trends. The direction it’s signalling this time? Run away from the Middle East. Japan buys 99.9 per cent of the oil it needs from overseas, mostly from the Middle East. Time to reassess. Bloomberg Where Japan goes, others in Asia would too. Indeed, South Korea, another major energy importer, has already announced plans to reduce its reliance on the Middle East. India has been less vocal but was trying to diversify even before the war in Iran. Beyond creating a major conundrum for Middle Eastern suppliers, the shift goes against geographic, economic and historic reasoning.

Advertisement

The Middle East and Far East are relatively close, so it makes commercial sense — particularly when the cost of shipping is high, as it is now — that oil flows from one region to the other. And so it has done for decades. Despite its deep sense of energy vulnerability after the 1973-74 oil crisis, and again in 1979, Japan trusted the Middle East, buying more than 90 per cent of its crude from the region. With the benefit of hindsight, the policy was — to borrow a phrase from Nobuo Tanaka, a former senior energy official in Japan who later ran the International Energy Agency — a “mistake”. If the mantra in the 1970s and 1980s was ‘get oil out of electricity,’ the next objective should be more radical: get oil out of transportation. The official message is, of course, more diplomatic. But read between the lines, and it’s obvious that Japanese officials are trying to rectify what they see as a policy failure. The key is “diversifying procurement sources and transport routes”, according to a cabinet document. The goal, while unquantified, is clear: to “break free from a structural vulnerability where recurring energy supply instability and constraints act as a bottleneck for Japan’s economic growth”. To be sure, the documents also talk about supporting construction of new pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which would allow it to keep buying crude from, say, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia without having to worry as much about instability in Iran. But Japan still looks to be headed for a major supply shift.

Advertisement

The Japanese government is discussing the plan, and a formal announcement including import targets and taxpayer money to support it may come before year-end. Seoul, meanwhile, has already set a quota and vows to reduce its oil supply from any region to 50 per cent of the total. Currently, the Middle East accounts for just over 75 per cent of South Korean oil imports. Related Article Petrol prices Australian fuel prices near six-month highs on US-Iran peace deal impasse Japan may not have the numbers sorted, but it isn’t waiting for the end of the war to make changes. In July, according to the latest monthly data available, the US was its main provider of oil, accounting for 37 per cent of total petroleum imports. It’s worth repeating because it reflects the power of the US shale revolution along with the latest upheaval in the global oil market: Washington is today the biggest oil supplier to Tokyo. Mexico and Latin America provided another 3 per cent. Turning those one-off statistics into sustained flows won’t be easy. But if history serves as any guide, Japan has demonstrated it can shift its oil consumption when it senses its national security is at stake. Back in the late 1970s, the country consumed more than 5.5 million barrels a day, generating more than 60 per cent of its electricity burning crude and fuel-oil. Betting heavily on coal, nuclear and liquefied natural gas, it pushed oil out of its power industry almost entirely. By 2025, Japanese oil consumption had fallen to a 55-year low of less than 3 million barrels a day.

Advertisement

Reducing dependency on the Middle East would be easier if overall Japanese oil demand drops further. The fewer barrels it needs to buy, the easier it is to shift purchases. If the mantra in the 1970s and 1980s was “get oil out of electricity,” the next objective should be more radical: get oil out of transportation. Japan gave the world the first mass-produced hybrid car, Toyota’s Prius. But in terms of electric cars, it’s lagging countries like China. AP It was Japan that gave the world the first mass-produced hybrid car, Toyota’s Prius. Hybrids have made huge inroads since then, helping to reduce gasoline consumption by about half over the last two decades. But Japan, the world’s fourth-largest car market by sales totals, lags in adoption of pure electric vehicles. Having developed hybrids first, its car manufacturers didn’t push nearly as hard as China’s into full electrification. The result is that today only about 2 per cent of new cars sales in Japan are full EVs, well below the 28 per cent average in Europe, and even trailing the US and Canada. The International Energy Agency believes the high share of the population living in apartments with limited access to private parking, in combination with a limited charging network, are constraining EV sales in Japan. That makes EVs an important lever for reducing oil imports, which would make diversification easier. So alongside its plans to finance pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, Tokyo should work harder to boost EV sales, with a focus on expanding its EV charging infrastructure.

Advertisement

It also should try to reduce oil usage in heating. Rural Japan relies on kerosene stoves, an oddity among industrialised nations. If Tokyo manages to squeeze down its gasoline and kerosene demand, what would be left is diesel and other petrochemical feedstock. (As the world’s fourth-largest chemicals producer, it imports huge amounts of refined petroleum products used in plastics and other materials.) Related Article Exclusive

Blood Oil Funding Putin: ‘Blood oil’ imports from major Asian supplier surge The oil market’s algebra, however, is unyieldingly zero-sum. If Japan succeeds, it will have to elbow its way into markets others consider their own, like West Africa and the Americas, the traditional hunting grounds of European refiners. And producers in the Middle East would need to find new customers. Trouble is, who would like to boost its reliance on Middle Eastern oil? I draw a blank. That wouldn’t be Tokyo’s problem to solve. But it’s another way in which Japan could change the global oil map for good.

Advertisement

Three years after it was mothballed, national brick maker Brickworks will restart operations at its Austral Bricks facility in Cardup, south of Perth, with the help of taxpayers. The state government will spend $4 million to restart operations at the Cardup plant and boost brick production in WA by 10 to 15 per cent in a bid to address the state’s crippling shortage, which has home builders fearing for their futures. WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti. Ross Swanborough The money will include a $3 million payment to Brickworks to recommission equipment at the Cardup site as well as a $500,000 payment to ensure the plant resumes operations by March. Another $500,000 payment will be made if Brickworks can deliver 17 million maxibricks – which are used in internal walls and general construction – within the first year of operations.

Advertisement

Perth home builders have been warning the state government for months of a looming a brick shortage in the state after Midland Brick began rationing bricks. “This is a time where we can’t allow this situation to roll on without doing anything,” Treasurer Rita Saffioti said on Tuesday. “Something needs to be done. We see the urgency. The building industry, in particular, have been very clear. “We need to get more bricks as soon as possible to ensure this doesn’t become a major challenge that exists for years upon years.” Even the state’s biggest builders like Dale Alcock of the ABN Group are struggling to get bricks to service their huge pipeline of work

Advertisement

Advertisement

He said 17 million maxibricks was the capacity of the plant, which it was running at in 2021-22. Ellenor said the March timeframe was tight but achievable, and they had already deployed engineers and operations staff from the East Coast to start the recommissioning. “The time frame is tight but all going well we will have bricks being produced in late March. The main challenge will be employing 35 workers in the Byford area,” he said. Alcock said he would go as far as to say that Brickworks’ new facility would still not produce enough bricks to meet demand, “but it’s certainly a large help.” The state government has poured about $100 million into boosting alternative construction methods to reduce the state’s obsession with double brick.

Advertisement

However, Alcock said WA was still a double brick state. “We talk about different methods of construction. We’re up for that, but you can’t just change your construction methodology overnight as an industry,” he said. “I encourage the government to undertake whatever support they can to Midland Brick and to Brickworks to try and increase capacity over the coming years because we are a double brick state and we need bricks.” Alcock said his company had about 100 jobs with slabs down, but no bricks loaded on them. “It’s taking us about an average of about four to six weeks to get brick supply,” he said.

Advertisement

Housing Industry Association WA boss Michael McGowan said 70 per cent of homes in the state were built using the double brick construction method. He said there would likely still be delays over the next 12 months and asked customers to be patient with builders and trades. Home Builders Action Group chairman Jason Janssen has been raising the industries concerns for months and said, while he welcomed the news that Cardup was restarting, it wouldn’t be enough. “It gives us hope from March to next year but between now and then there is a lot of uncertainty,” he said. Janssen called on the state government to switch the majority of its public housing build program, which includes thousands of dwellings, from double brick to alternative construction methods to free up bricks in the private market.

title: AFL considering changes to free agency system
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 AFL considering changes to free agency system Jake Niall Updated September 29, 2026 — 1:52pm ,first published 12:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL will consider changes to free agency in the interests of ensuring that the system does not skew the competitive balance of the competition in favour of the teams in premiership contention. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon confirmed that the league would discuss potential changes to the free agency rules to make sure that the competitive balance of the 18 clubs was not distorted. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has flagged potential changes to free agency. Eddie Jim “Look, I think it’s been in place for now probably 12 or 14 years,” the AFL boss told this masthead in grand final week. “I think what we’re seeing in the last couple of years is what everyone thought would happen at the start, and it didn’t necessarily. “But it’s something that we’ll talk with the players association about because competitive balance is really important. That you know, we do a lot of work around the draft, we do a lot of work around the salary cap, a lot of work around the soft cap.”

Advertisement

Asked if the AFL would consider changes to free agency, Dillon said: “Yeah, with the agreement [with the players], just to make sure that the competitive balance isn’t distorted.” The potential to reform free agency – which was introduced for 2012 and has been the subject of minor changes and ongoing debate – comes as the Brisbane Lions, once stragglers, won their third flag on end in their fourth consecutive grand final. They attracted both Sam Draper and Oscar Allen from lowly Essendon and West Coast, respectively, as free agents, albeit the Eagles received a generous pick No.2 for their ex-skipper. The AFL wanted to change the compensation system at the end of last year to remove compensation picks inside the top 10, and thus not compromise the draft for teams who weren’t finalists (not counting the new wildcards). But the AFL Players’ Association resisted that change, and the status quo remained. As a result, Port Adelaide can receive pick No.5 in return for departing superstar free agent Zak Butters and Gold Coast can gain pick No.7 for key forward Ben King, who is crossing to Hawthorn.

Advertisement

These deals give the clubs losing the star arguably superior compensation compared to what they could gain in a trade if they choose to match the free agent offers. The AFL is closely watching the side deals that those clubs – the Western Bulldogs and Port, Hawthorn and Gold Coast – propose, to make sure that they are “commercial” and reflect market value. Related Article Opinion

AFL grand final Why three-peat Hawks and another super side have Fagan’s Heroes covered Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age One potential reform, which is likely to be canvassed, is a rule that forces the top teams to give up a draft pick, such as their first pick, for a high-value free agent. Under that reform, Hawthorn, as a top four team, would lose their first draft pick for King, and still land him as a free agent. This could potentially apply to the top four, top six or top eight teams from that season. Most of the most prized free agents have gone to teams that had been in premiership contention. These include Lance Franklin (Sydney), Patrick Dangerfield (Geelong), Tom Lynch (Richmond), Jeremy Cameron (Geelong) and Joe Daniher (Brisbane Lions). It is rare for a restricted free agent to opt for a team in the bottom six or eight. Older superstars Lachie Neale and Toby Greene are joining Collingwood and Geelong respectively as unrestricted free agents this year.

Advertisement

The position on free agency varies among clubs. Some would argue that it should be less restricted, others that the system is skewed towards teams in premiership contention. AFL free agency is enshrined in the players’ collective bargaining agreement and needs the players’ union’s consent to be altered in that agreement. The union has consistently opposed any measures that impede the ability of players to cross to their preferred club after a period of service. “The current free agency parameters mean only a small number of players take advantage of it each year. That makes it very competitive to attract free agents that become available,” AFLPA boss James Gallagher said. “Choice of club is important for players with relatively short career spans who don’t choose where their careers start. “Free agency has a role in competitive balance but that needs to be considered alongside other factors like the draft and its compromises, other player movement mechanisms and the soft cap.

Orbit Resources has hit two broad zones of strong sulphide mineralisation in an ongoing diamond drilling program at its 148-square-kilometre Lewis Ponds gold, silver and base metals project in New South Wales’ revered Lachlan Fold Belt. The company says one hole, designed to grow its existing resource, has visually identified two significant sulphide zones at the project’s Tom’s Lode prospect. The intercepts include a 12.9-metre zone containing 20 per cent semi-massive sulphides from 347.6m downhole and a separate 8.5-metre hit of stringer and disseminated sulphides from 326m. A diamond drill rig at work during the 2026 drilling campaign at Orbit Resources’ (formerly Godolphin Resources) flagship Lewis Ponds project near Orange in NSW. While assays are yet to confirm the grade, Orbit says the visual sulphide assemblage is encouraging, comprising pyrite, sphalerite, chalcopyrite, pyrrhotite and galena, the key ore minerals for zinc, copper and lead. The drilling forms part of a four-hole, 1500-metre campaign aimed at increasing confidence in the existing mineral resource, potentially converting inferred tonnes to the indicated category. It will also provide core for metallurgical test work. The hole that delivered the sulphide hits is still in progress, and once complete, the rig will move on to test the Spicer’s Lode to the north.

Advertisement

‘The current drilling program is focused on increasing geological confidence within the existing mineral resource.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens Additionally, a second hole has been completed to a depth of 400.2 metres, extending drilling deep into the Lewis Ponds footwall to test what might be lurking below. Samples have been sent to the lab, with results expected in the fourth quarter of this year. Meanwhile, the company has flown a drone aeromag survey across Lewis Ponds and its exploration corridor, including the fresh Cousin Jack discovery. The 40-metre line spacing program is expected to provide the company with data far superior to historical datasets, with validation and processing now underway to support future exploration targeting. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “To date, one drill hole has intersected Tom’s Lode broadly in the position predicted by our geological model, providing encouraging support for our geological interpretation in this part of the deposit. The two visually identified sulphide zones demonstrate the continuity of the mineralised system, while pending assays will be important in determining the grade and metal distribution associated with these intersections and their significance to the existing Mineral Resource.” The Lewis Ponds project, just 15km east of Orange, already hosts a formidable JORC-compliant resource of 17.52 million tonnes grading 1.12 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, 53.34g/t silver, 2.06 per cent zinc, 1.10 per cent lead and 0.14 per cent copper. This equates to a combined 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent, including an impressive 630,000 ounces of gold and 30.1 million ounces of silver.

The current drill program is focused on expanding that polymetallic bounty and comes amid renewed interest in the Lachlan Fold Belt, where major players such as Regis Resources and C29 are chasing similar precious and base metal systems. The campaign follows on from previous exploration success, which included a discovery at the Cousin Jack prospect that jagged two broad sulphide zones of 79m at 1.3 per cent zinc equivalent and a hefty 104m grading 1.3 per cent zinc equivalent. Those hits also featured a higher-grade 1.7-metre intercept grading an eye-catching 13.1 per cent zinc equivalent. Notably, another hole drilled earlier this year hit the Quarry Lode, a zone of mineralisation sitting outside the deposit’s current resource boundary, with an intercept of 27 metres at 0.97g/t gold equivalent from 83m. The company believes bringing the Quarry Lode into the inventory could increase the project’s scale and support future mining studies. Beyond its flagship project, Orbit has plenty waiting in the wings, with almost 1700 square kilometres of gold-copper ground spread across the broader Orange region. The company’s Mt Aubrey prospect, 35km northeast of Parkes, has an inferred resource of 1.21Mt at 1.61g/t gold for 62,400 ounces. Meanwhile, its Copper Hill East target offers a different prize: the hunt for a major porphyry system. Sitting just 30km north of Molong, the 8km copper-gold corridor is less than 10km from Golden Cross Resources’ Copper Hill porphyry deposit, which hosts 280,000 tonnes of copper and 750,000 ounces of gold.

Orbit also retains a free-carried interest in the Yeoval-Goodrich copper-gold joint venture, where Great Plains Metals is earning up to 70 per cent, giving the company another shot at a porphyry discovery without footing the whole exploration bill. With the drill rods turning on a campaign to build on an already substantial resource at Lewis Ponds, the visual confirmation of more sulphides where the geological model says they should be is a welcome sight. While assays will tell the full story, the combination of a significant existing resource, recent discoveries and a deep pipeline of prospects suggests Orbit has a full dance card in one of Australia’s most prospective mineral provinces. title: The unlikely Australian Black Summer landmark that's been classified as a national treasure
text:
In brief A public telephone that became a lifeline for a small town during the Black Summer bushfires has been heritage-listed.

The landline phone put through over 1,000 calls from locals when power and mobile services failed.

Under furious orange skies and plumes of bushfire smoke, locals and tourists lined up at a public phone to talk to family and friends or check in on neighbours.

Some used the public phone in Narooma to tell loved ones they were safe, while others revealed they had lost everything in the catastrophic Black Summer bushfires that razed much of the NSW far south coast.

Historian Naomi Parry Duncan was holidaying in Narooma on New Year's Day in 2020, among those who had to shelter at an evacuation centre as the fires loomed.

There was no mobile reception or power during that "bewildering and frightening" time, sending many to wait at three public phones in town, Parry Duncan recalled.

"At all of the pay phones there were queues of people politely waiting," she told the Australian Associated Press news agency.

"It was quite an intimate space in the queue."

The phone outside Narooma Plaza on the Princes Highway has been heritage-listed for its cultural and social role in the Black Summer fires, with almost 1,000 calls made over two months during and after the disaster.

Parry Duncan led the nomination to the National Trust of Australia NSW register.

The phone is now marked with the trust's bronze plaque, emblazoned with gum leaves, to denote its significance.

During the fires, long queues of locals and tourists would form to use the pay phone at Narooma. Source: AAP / Supplied / PR image

The quiet empathy displayed by people waiting for the phones as they carried shared trauma was a particularly moving sight, Parry Duncan said.

"The instinctive thing to help each other was really quite amazing," she said.

Her New Zealand-born partner saw the way people waited patiently for the phone and felt a deeper understanding of Australia, she said.

READ MORE Covering the Black Summer Bushfires: Lara Coffey

The landmark status was being sought for other phones, including one in remote Queensland and another in Melbourne.

Telstra is mandated to maintain Australia's 14,000 pay phones, with all local and national calls to standard fixed lines and mobiles free since mid-2021.

Within the last year, 25 million calls have been made from pay phones, including 300,000 to triple zero and crisis support lines.

"Where we've got vulnerable people in the community out there who need crisis support and to stay connected, they're showing us these pay phones are absolutely critical," Telstra regional general manager Chris Taylor said.

Telstra has been working to ensure better resilience during disasters, such as power back-ups to help restore connectivity more quickly, Taylor said.

Parry Duncan said public phones have a long history in Australian culture, playing a particularly important part in women's lives.

The phones were used to help women find employment and leave abusive relationships throughout the last century, as well as keeping Indigenous communities connected, she said.

"They are so important for keeping us together, especially when you've got a country that is spread over such vast distances as Australia."

title: RBA hikes rates to 15-year high amid rising energy costs — as it happened
text:
Meanwhile, overseas ...

How are other countries handling global inflationary pressures?

New Zealand

Across the Tasman, New Zealand is also grappling with inflation. On 2 September, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raised the official cash rate by 0.25 percentage points to 2.75 per cent.

Inflation there has been climbing steeply: annual inflation hit 4.1 per cent in the year to June, up from 3.1 per cent in March.

United States

On 17 September, the US also hiked interest rates by 0.25 percentage points. Policymakers there say another rate hike is likely to follow.

US President Donald Trump wasn't pleased.

"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!," he posted on X.

United Kingdom

The story is different in the UK, where interest rates have been left unchanged at 3.75 per cent six times in a row. Inflation peaked at 11 per cent in 2022 in the UK and has been trending downwards since — although February's attacks on Iran have started pushing inflation up there too.

Before the war, rates had been expected to fall, but instead they have stayed steady. Analysts say the Bank of England will likely need to increase rates there too by the end of the year.

Europe

Euro-zone inflation has soared past 3 per cent and may approach 4 per cent by the end of the year, double the European Central Bank's target.

Markets there are anticipating another rate rise in December— the current short-term policy rate is at 2.5 per cent.

title: What a reported weapons offer reveals about the complexities of US-China ties
text:
In brief Donald Trump denied asking Xi Jinping to buy US weapons, contradicting remarks by his ambassador to China.

The confusion fuelled scrutiny of US-China policy as officials insisted no arms sales to China were planned.

US President Donald Trump has disputed that he asked Chinese leader Xi Jinping if he wanted to buy weapons from the United States, contradicting an account from the US ambassador to China.

Trump on Tuesday acted confused when a reporter asked him about ambassador David Perdue's remarks over the weekend, suggesting the diplomat was confusing China with Taiwan. But then Trump said "maybe it's a good idea" to make such an offer to China.

The whiplash over the prospect of arms sales from the US to its ascendant geopolitical rival underlines the Trump administration's often uncoordinated and contradictory approach to China, including Xi's pomp-filled state visit to Washington DC last week, during which Trump appeared to get little in return on key issues.

Perdue, speaking to Shannon Bream on the Fox News Sunday program days after the summit, didn’t specify when the offer was made. But such a proposal, if realised, would upend generations of US policy toward China and Taiwan and expose US technology to a potential foe.

China or Taiwan?

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The US State Department on Tuesday looked to distance the Trump administration from Perdue's comments, saying that "US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China."

Hours later, Trump seemed to be doing the same.

"To China? You mean to Taiwan?" he said when a reporter asked him about Perdue's account.

"I never heard of that one. I’m going to have to ask him," Trump said.

He then mused that China would probably like to buy US equipment, which he said was superior, and added: "So maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss it. He may have been talking about Taiwan. I think he was probably talking about Taiwan."

Perdue said Sunday that the Republican president was downplaying longstanding US arms sales to Taiwan — which have drawn protest from Beijing for years — by couching it as just one of many sales the US makes around the world, and even asking Xi if he’d be in the market for US weaponry.

Bream had cited concerns from Republican and Democratic politicians over delayed aid packages and weapons orders to Taiwan, the self-ruled democracy that seeks to defend itself from China’s threat to invade the island. Bream asked if the US is denying arms to Taiwan to appease the Chinese president.

Perdue pushed back on the suggestion, stating that Trump "is as strong on Taiwan as I’ve ever seen anybody" and has sold it plenty of weapons. Perdue also said Trump and Xi continue to talk about future US weapons sales to Taiwan.

"But President Trump continues to say, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,'" Perdue said. "He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point."

‘Trump’s transactional worldview'

If so, that offer "speaks to (Trump's) treatment of China in almost exclusively commercial terms, even at the potential expense of the US military position in Asia," said Evan Sankey, an analyst focused on US policy toward China at the libertarian Cato Institute.

He said the US last sold arms to Beijing in the 1980s and resuming those sales would be "a shocking policy change."

Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the hawkish think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the anecdote that Perdue told offers “a revealing window into Trump's transactional worldview.”

"He tends to see weapons, tariffs and market access as instruments of leverage, even across the traditional dividing line between allies and adversaries," Singleton said.

Such an offer to Xi also would come in contrast with US obligations under a domestic law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself and deter invasion from Beijing, which has vowed to seize the island by force if necessary. While not recognising Taiwan as a country, the US is the island’s strongest informal backer and primary arms provider. But multiple US leaders have left it ambiguous whether they would commit military force to defend the island should China invade.

China has pressed the US to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a previous summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the US paused the sale of a record-breaking US$14 billion ($19.9 billion) package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a "very good negotiating chip" with China.

In their private talks at the White House last week, Xi pressed Trump to oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did not confirm Perdue's remarks when asked about the matter on Monday. But he told reporters that China has always strengthened its national defence capabilities based on its needs and is committed to maintaining world peace and stability.

title: The numbers every mortgage borrower and hopeful buyer should know
text:
In brief Interest rates are likely to rise for the fourth time this year.

How much more will you pay, how much less could you borrow, and what number should your interest rate have in front of it?

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is widely expected to raise interest rates on Tuesday for the fourth time this year, taking the nation's cash rate to a 15-year high.

The RBA has signalled it will target persistent high inflation, driven in part by the Middle East conflict, the surging global demand for AI-related technology and stronger-than-expected spending at home.

The pain will be felt by existing borrowers and prospective homebuyers alike.

For many mortgage borrowers, another 0.25 percentage point increase would add to monthly repayments that have already soared by hundreds of dollars this year.

For Australians trying to enter the property market, another hike could shave thousands off the amount they can borrow.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

How much could another rate hike cost you?

According to analysis by financial comparison site Canstar, a standard rate rise on Tuesday would add roughly $107 to the monthly repayments on a $700,000 loan on an average variable rate, bringing the cumulative increase this year to $424 a month.

For a mortgage of $1 million, monthly repayments would rise by $152, bringing the total monthly increase this year to $606.

"This could well be the straw that breaks the camel's back for some [borrowers]," Sally Tindall, Canstar's data insights director, told SBS News.

A recent survey by financial comparison site Money.com.au found 39 per cent of respondents were not confident they could continue to afford mortgage repayments if rates rise in September, with 9 per cent suggesting they might have to seriously consider selling their properties.

While the Commonwealth Bank, Westpac and NAB are forecasting just one more hike this year — bringing the cash rate to 4.60 per cent by the end of 2026 — ANZ is projecting two more hikes, in September and November, bringing the cash rate to 4.85 per cent.

If the RBA raises rates again in November, Canstar estimates repayments would rise by a further $107 a month on a $700,000 loan and $153 on a $1 million loan.

That would take the total increase in monthly repayments across five rate rises this year to $532 and $759 respectively.

One in five respondents in Money.com.au's survey said they would be forced to consider selling if there are two more standard rate hikes.

How could a hike affect those trying to buy?

Higher interest rates don't just increase repayments for existing home loan borrowers — they can also reduce how much banks will lend to new borrowers.

If rates rise again, Tindall says people looking to get into the property market will find that their maximum home-buying budget "has taken yet another haircut".

"It could be back to the drawing board for some people. It could force even more prospective home buyers onto the sidelines for the remainder of the year, maybe potentially even into next year," she said.

A standard rate hike on Tuesday could cut an average wage earner's borrowing power by $11,200, according to Canstar analysis — a total fall of 9 per cent since the start of the year.

For a couple, that figure doubles to $22,400, bringing the total reduction this year to $94,700.

Should rates rise twice before the end of the year, this year's hikes will have shaved a total of $116,200 from a couple's borrowing power.

What can borrowers do?

Existing borrowers may be able to offset some of the impact by ensuring they're paying a competitive mortgage rate.

Canstar estimates the average variable rate for an owner-occupier paying principal and interest would rise to 6.49 per cent if Tuesday's expected hike is passed on in full.

But more competitive rates could still be available, with Canstar defining anything below 6.25 per cent as competitive after a rate hike, and the lowest variable rate on the market estimated at 5.94 per cent.

Estimated variable rates if the cash rate rises to 4.6 per cent on Tuesday.

Tindall said borrowers should check how their rate compares with the market and with the rate their lender is offering to new customers.

"If your bank is offering a more competitive rate to new customers rather than you as a loyal existing one, you can ring them up and call them out on it," she suggested.

"Also have a couple of rates up your sleeve from other lenders."

If their bank won't budge, borrowers could consider refinancing with another lender, though Tindall said it was worth negotiating with their existing lender first given the additional paperwork and fees that can come with switching.

Mortgage broker aggregator Loan Market Group reported refinancing activity was up 14.9 per cent in September compared with the weekly average in August.

For borrowers who are worried they won't be able to meet their repayments, Tindall said they should consider contacting their lender as early as possible to discuss what hardship assistance may be available.

Options can include temporarily pausing repayments, switching to interest-only repayments for a period, or extending the loan term to reduce monthly repayments.

However, Tindall cautioned that some of these measures could leave borrowers paying more over the longer term, and recommended seeking independent financial advice before agreeing to any hardship arrangement.

"No one really wants to make that phone call, but if you're in that position, it's really important to do it and do it before you miss a repayment," she said. "They are required to help you."

title: Treasurer Jim Chalmers touts stronger budget amid darkening economic outlook
text:
In brief Australia’s 2025-26 budget deficit came in about $6 billion better than forecast, driven by stronger investment and super income.

The improved result was overshadowed by expectations of a fresh RBA rate rise as oil prices fuel inflation fears.

Australia's budget has finished about $6 billion better off in the 2025/26 financial year, the government has revealed, as it braces for a damaging interest rate rise.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher touted their fiscal credentials when they released the final budget outcome on Monday, but also face difficult questions about an increasingly gloomy economic outlook.

Chalmers noted that today's improvements did not come from higher taxes on wages or commodities.

"Mining profits came in lower than what was anticipated," he said.

"It is overwhelmingly from higher super and investor income than what we anticipated in the Treasury's forecasts in May."

Though he readily welcomed the government's improved bottom line, he conceded there are "difficult months" to come, acknowledging that interest rates are expected to rise when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) meets on Tuesday.

Gallagher confirmed the improvement to the underlying deficit, which was projected to be $28.3 billion in the May budget.

It's still a good deal worse than the previous year's final budget outcome, which put the deficit at just under $10 billion for 2024/25.

With deficits projected for another decade, and mortgage holders bracing for another Reserve Bank rate hike on Tuesday, Gallagher was forced to defend the role of government spending on inflation.

"We've found savings, including savings in an ongoing sense, to make sure that where government investment is happening, that it's not adding to the inflation challenge in our economy," she told ABC Radio National.

"But there is a war in the Middle East, and that war is having impacts not just at the petrol bowser, but across the board. The sooner that war ends, the better."

With inflation stubbornly above the RBA's 2-3 per cent target band, the Middle East oil shock is set to keep price pressures elevated for longer.

Brent oil futures lifted to US$106 a barrel as peace talks between the US and Iran hit another snag.

The shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, higher Chinese imports and softer exports from non-OPEC countries have further weakened the supply picture, said the Commonwealth Bank's head of commodities Vivek Dhar.

"If global oil and refined product inventories do deplete, Brent oil futures risk surging as high as US$150 a barrel to induce uncontrolled demand destruction (i.e. where high prices reduce demand) in emerging and developing Asian economies," he said.

Each US$1 increase in the Brent oil price roughly translates to a 1c increase in fuel prices at the bowser.

Those higher service station costs will likely nudge headline inflation from 3.5 to 4 per cent by the time the Australian Bureau of Statistics reports on Wednesday.

The US, Europe and Japan have all hiked interest rates due to rising fuel prices since the RBA met in August.

Hawkish comments from governor Michele Bullock and other top RBA officials in recent weeks have emphasised that the bank is losing patience with inflation and is likely to follow.

The bank's board is widely expected to lift the cash rate to 4.6 per cent when it wraps up its two-day meeting on Tuesday — the highest level in 15 years.

Liberal MP Zoe McKenzie sought to pin the inflation spike on government spending, despite growth in public demand moderating in recent years.

"The rest of the world is not experiencing the inflation that we are experiencing here at home," she told News24.

While drivers despair at the pump, auction clearance rates, a leading house price indicator, slumped to a 10-week preliminary low of 50.3 per cent on Sunday, according to housing data firm Cotality.

Median property prices nationwide have slumped 3.6 per cent since March's cyclical peak as the removal of tax concessions in May's budget combines with three consecutive rate hikes to cripple buyer confidence.

While Bullock has stressed interest rate decisions are not designed to target house prices, economists have linked lower house prices to consumers spending less across the board, tugging inflation down.

title: Does daylight saving mess with mental health? What to know before the clocks change
text:
In brief Daylight saving time starts on Sunday.

A new study examined how it affects mental health, amid overseas calls to end seasonal clock changes.

It's that time of year again. This weekend, millions of Australians trade an hour of sleep for more sunshine at the end of the day as daylight saving time (DST) begins.

For some, it signals the start of summery evenings in Australia and more light for after-work activities. For early risers, it could mean tougher wake-ups, with the sun rising later in the morning.

And then there's the disruption to sleep as the clocks move forward by an hour on Sunday — an adjustment often blamed for leaving people tired, irritable and out of sorts.

But new research suggests these disruptions don't necessarily translate into more serious mental health outcomes.

In an international review of existing research into a range of health and wellbeing effects associated with DST transitions, Swinburne University researchers focused specifically on outcomes including depression, bipolar disorder, dementia and seasonal affective disorder.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We found that there were no consistent or large effects on the transition to daylight saving time on these serious mental health outcomes," Ben Bullock, a senior lecturer and researcher at Swinburne University who specialises in psychology, sleep, mental health and circadian rhythms, told SBS News.

So what does that mean as the spring clock change approaches?

When does daylight saving time start, and where?

On Sunday 4 October, clocks in NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia, ACT and Norfolk Island will jump forward to 3am, costing people an hour of sleep in the process.

Queensland, Western Australia, Northern Territory, Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands do not observe daylight saving.

Daylight saving ends on Sunday 4 April at 3am, when clocks go back an hour.

New South Wales, Victoria, Australia, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory have all observed daylight saving since 1967.

Does daylight saving negatively affect your body?

Some sleep experts believe DST can negatively impact sleep, leading to other health risks.

Research suggests that sleep is crucial for mental and physical health, with chronic deprivation and disruption linked to mood changes, cardiovascular disease and impaired cognitive function.

The Sleep Health Foundation, for example, says DST can affect sleep patterns and overall wellbeing by disrupting the body's internal circadian rhythm and sleep-wake cycle.

According to the organisation, the springtime change of clocks is generally harder to adjust to than the one in autumn, when you gain an hour of sleep.

Sleep science organisations in the US, UK and Europe have previously called for seasonal clock changes to be abolished. In the US, President Donald Trump is pushing legislation to make DST permanent year-round across the country.

So, does daylight saving affect our mental health or not?

Bullock stressed the findings don't mean people can't feel the effects of the clock change.

Changes to the timing and availability of light can affect circadian rhythms and sleep, which can in turn influence mood and cognitive function.

But his research found little evidence that these effects translated into more serious mental health outcomes.

The review examined studies using hospital and other official records to measure serious mental health outcomes, including presentations involving depression, substance abuse and psychosis.

Bullock said the researchers wanted to examine whether the evidence supported significant policy changes such as the one proposed by several international sleep science groups.

"There are effects on sleep and circadian rhythms from changes in the available light and the timing of that light," he said.

"If we're going to get rid of something like daylight saving ... we need a stronger evidence base, and we just didn't find that it had that effect."

He said the broader review did, however, find small effects on some other health and wellbeing outcomes, including heart attacks and road accidents.

What can you do to get through the transition?

For those who struggle with the switch to daylight saving, Bullock said there are ways to make the adjustment easier.

In the days leading up to the change, he recommends gradually bringing your bedtime forward, rather than suddenly losing an hour on Sunday.

Getting outside into natural light early on Sunday morning can also help reset the body's internal clock.

"The third thing is to plan for the change and sort of be a bit gentle on yourself," he said.

"So don't plan any big things or big events, or expect to do lots of things on the Sunday after the transition."

"If you just look after yourself on that day, you will adjust slowly over the following few days. The body's pretty good at adjusting reasonably quickly, and it's quite resilient."

title: Hundreds of dollars a year: How Tuesday's RBA decision could affect borrowers
text:
In brief The RBA is due to make its next rates decision at 2.30pm on Tuesday.

The call could send interest rates up for the fourth time this year.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is poised to make its next cash rate decision, with all major financial institutions agreeing that a rate hike is all but inevitable.

The 'big four' banks and financial markets have priced in an 80 to 90 per cent probability of a 25 percentage point increase, pushing the cash rate from 4.35 per cent to 4.6 per cent — its highest level since 2011.

The RBA is expected to view inflation risks as materialising faster and higher than previously forecast, demanding another rate hike.

The prolonged conflict in the Middle East, which has escalated and expanded in recent weeks, has pushed Brent crude oil prices to their highest level in months.

Domestic demand, GDP growth, and employment have proven to be far more resilient than expected, while Australia's productivity remains sluggish.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The latest figures, which will be updated on Tuesday, show headline inflation is 3.5 per cent, while the trimmed mean — a measure of inflation that removes the biggest price swings — sits at 3.6 per cent.

Fuel costs, housing construction, and dining out expenses are the main drivers of inflation at present, Australian Bureau of Statistics data show, pushing it well above the RBA's 2 to 3 per cent target.

Richard Witten, money expert at the comparison site Finder, told SBS News that Australia is at the mercy of "global inflationary pressures" with little agency over the issue, but that the RBA "has a mandate to keep inflation down" and that "their main tool for doing that is rate rises".

The big four predict the RBA decision

This is the first time in this current cycle that all four of Australia's major trading banks — Commonwealth Bank (CBA), Westpac, National Australia Bank (NAB), and ANZ — are forecasting a 0.25 per cent increase.

ANZ economists have said the RBA no longer views recent energy price spikes as a temporary blip, but as a broader, long-term inflationary risk they want to suppress. It has already predicted back-to-back rate rises, with another hike coming in November.

ANZ and the other big four banks are predicting the RBA will increase the cash rate for the fourth time this year on Tuesday. Source: AAP / Esther Linder

Westpac and CBA both brought their November hike prediction forward to this month. While they believe 4.6 per cent is the likely peak this cycle, both will be watching the RBA's explanation closely.

CBA said that if Tuesday's data shows a quarterly trimmed mean inflation rise of 1 per cent or more, a second rate hike in November will likely be triggered.

NAB said a single 0.25 per cent increase is the likely scenario, although a follow-up increase does remain a risk depending on labour data.

What another rate rise means for borrowers

If banks fully pass on the 0.25 per cent increase, borrowers can expect to pay hundreds of dollars more to service their loans.

The average home loan in Australia currently sits at $731,000, ranging from an average of $516,000 in Tasmania to $842,000 in NSW, according to ABS and Canstar data. First home buyers hold an average loan of $610,000.

The current average variable rate is between 6.24 and 6.62 per cent for owner-occupiers, meaning the average Australian is spending $4,500 to $4,680 per month on their mortgage.

A 0.25 per cent increase would add $120 per month to the average home loan, or $1,440 per year.

The average NSW borrower will pay an additional $138 per month, or $1,656 per year, while the average first home buyer will pay an additional $100 per month or $1,200 per year.

A 0.25 per cent increase also lowers the maximum borrowing capacity for new buyers by roughly 2 to 2.5 per cent, as bank serviceability buffers shift higher.

Renters are not immune, as property investors with variable loans are further incentivised to pass on these additional mortgage costs in a low-vacancy market where alternatives are scarce. The current national rental vacancy rate sits at 1.2 per cent.

Mortgage stress on the rise

Research from the polling group Roy Morgan shows that 29 per cent of Australian mortgage holders — around 1.54 million people — are currently classified as "at risk" of mortgage stress.

On average, servicing a new mortgage requires around 45 per cent of household income, up from 29.6 per cent in 2020.

Witten from Finder noted that while low interest rates were common around the globe for the decade or so before the pandemic, central banks are now raising rates to a "more historically normal" level.

"It's more challenging today though than in 2011," he said. "The amount you have to borrow now is much, much higher, so the same interest rate is much, much more expensive and punishing today than it was back then."

Finder's borrower survey data has not shown a major increase in mortgage defaults or distressed property sales, however Witten said that could change.

"The average borrower still has some sort of savings buffer they're relying on, but it does seem to be getting thinner," he said. "People will report higher feelings of mortgage stress, struggling to repay their home loan."

"They'll say to us in surveys that 'one more rate hike will put me over the edge'."

While the RBA is trying to keep inflation down, pushing rates higher risks triggering a recession as borrowers pull back on spending — something Bullock has previously noted the RBA is highly attuned to.

Witten said the central bank believes "borrowers can handle the hikes", but that a cash rate of 4.85 per cent may be as high as it's willing to go.

"Then it becomes a conversation around, 'does the government itself need to step in?' Because rate rises are just not working."

The RBA will announce its decision at 2.30pm on Tuesday, with Bullock holding a live media conference at 3.30pm.

title: A tiny camera. A hidden earpiece. And someone waiting outside the exam room
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

During the June exam period, University of Sydney student Charlotte (not her real name) left an economics exam relieved it was over.

She was already thinking about the exams she had left and the holiday that would follow.

Then she opened Douyin.

On the Chinese social media platform, she found a screenshot of some questions from the exam she had just sat.

The images were being used as promotional material by sellers of covert equipment, who claimed they demonstrated how their cameras could capture exam papers in real time from inside exam rooms. The University of Sydney later confirmed that material from 10 subjects had been leaked using hidden cameras during the June exam period.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Someone had posted some of the questions from the exam.

"The post had 'ECON1001' — the University of Sydney course code — written on it, along with hashtags for the university and 'final'," Charlotte tells SBS Chinese.

The "first-person view" exam footage promoted by sellers shows a question paper for a University of Sydney economics course. Credit: SBS

Charlotte had seen advertisements for the technology before — small cameras disguised as buttons, paired with wireless earpieces, designed to be used without attracting the attention of exam supervisors.

"Some of these cameras can vibrate. They can vibrate a certain number of times to indicate the answer choice," she says.

As technology makes it easier to capture and transmit exam material, universities face a new challenge: how to maintain exam integrity when questions can leave the room almost as quickly as students do.

Inside the exam cheating market

Following the University of Sydney exam leak, SBS Chinese searched Douyin using keywords including "Australian exams" and identified dozens of accounts advertising button-sized devices designed to secretly photograph exam papers.

Many accounts posted so-called "first-person footage" as a promotional tactic.

As part of our investigation, an SBS Chinese reporter posed as an international student and approached five random sellers on the platform. All said they could provide a complete cheating setup consisting of a button camera and a wireless earpiece "the size of a grain of rice", with the equipment available to either rent or buy.

Rental prices ranged from 3,000 yuan ($626) to 5,000 yuan ($1,044), while buying the equipment cost between 8,000 yuan ($1,672) and 11,000 yuan ($2,298).

One seller said: "The camera transmits the footage, while the earpiece is used to hear the answers. Once the camera captures the exam paper, we can see it on our end and then transmit the answers to you through the earpiece."

Button cameras marketed as tools for cheating in university exams are being promoted across multiple social media platforms. Credit: SBS

The seller said the students could either find someone themselves to answer the questions or pay an additional fee for "teachers who have graduated in the same discipline" to provide real-time assistance during the exam.

"Go with our teachers and the exam is guaranteed. Even though the University of Sydney has tightened its rules, our clients still pass," they said.

Another seller said the service would typically involve three "teachers" helping one student — two answering questions in real time and a third reading the answers to the student through the earpiece.

A third seller claimed to have sold more than 10 sets of the equipment in June alone.

The sellers assured the devices were "extremely discreet", with the camera designed to look like an ordinary button.

They also offered to provide training before the exam to show students how to set up the equipment and test that it was working properly.

Some sellers on select social media platforms are marketing high-tech cheating devices to students for use in university exams. Credit: Europa Press via Getty Images

The University of Sydney says it has made progress in its investigation into the June cheating incident, but declined to say how many students it is investigating.

A university spokesperson told SBS Chinese: "In this exam period and on previous occasions, we've identified a number of 'cheating jackets' with hidden cameras used to take photographs of exam papers, to be relayed via a connected device to someone outside the venue."

"These cheating companies are predatory and brazen. We've increased our support to students so they can seek help and report any approaches or suspicious behaviour."

The university said anyone found to have engaged in misconduct would face significant consequences under its disciplinary procedures.

How technology is changing exam cheating

Australia's higher education regulator says commercial academic cheating remains a persistent problem.

By December 2024, the federal government's Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) had blocked 422 websites offering illegal academic cheating services, including businesses that arrange for someone else to complete assessments on behalf of students.

Meena Jha, an associate professor at CQ University's School of Engineering and Technology, who has researched academic integrity in higher education, says the technology available to students is also changing.

She says new wearable technologies can include smart glasses, micro-earpieces and screen-enabled pens.

Associate professor Meena Jha says exam cheating has evolved alongside advances in technology. Source: SBS News

"If they are internet-connected, they can transmit data in real time while they are sitting, writing, doing the exam," Jha tells SBS Chinese.

It is real-time misconduct. It is not only one individual who is being involved here. It's probably the entire class.

Jha says the University of Sydney incident reflects a wider challenge for universities as the technology becomes more accessible.

"These technologies are available and as the technological costs are going down, they will be more available to our students," she says.

"These are quite alarming things and how universities are trying to grapple or to address these issues is a challenge."

The challenge is not limited to Australia. Regulators and education providers overseas are also dealing with the use of phones and other connected devices.

In the United Kingdom, exam regulator Ofqual reported 2,225 cases of student malpractice involving mobile phones and smart devices in tertiary and senior school exams in 2025, accounting for 44.3 per cent of all cheating cases.

The business after students are caught

For some students, the problems begin after the exam.

SBS Chinese found that after the University of Sydney exam incident, some academic appeals agencies started posting on social media, offering services to students facing university investigations.

These commercial agencies claim to help students accused of academic misconduct prepare for university hearings and appeals. Their services can also extend to other university matters, including applications to withdraw from subjects after the usual deadline, grade or assessment appeals, special consideration, and enrolment or course progression disputes.

But the services can be expensive, and the outcome is not guaranteed.

Faye (not her real name), an international student at Monash University, was one of those who sought help to improve her overall grade.

In January, concerned that a subject result could affect her future studies, Faye was introduced to an agency offering what it described as an "exceptional withdrawal" service.

She paid 4,500 yuan ($939).

Faye (not her real name), a student at Monash University, paid more than $1,500 for an academic appeals service, but her appeal ultimately failed.

The agency proposed that she apply for an exceptional withdrawal by providing medical evidence that she had experienced special circumstances while studying the subject.

"They said they had partnerships with local hospitals [in China], and that I could specify which hospital I wanted. They could contact them and arrange a certificate," Faye tells SBS Chinese.

The agency told her mental health issues were among the most common grounds for such applications.

They said, 'Because you were not in a good state and it affected your studies. That's the reason to apply.'

The medical certificate and its NAATI (National Accreditation Authority for Translators and Interpreters) translation cost an additional 2,750 yuan ($573), bringing the total to 7,250 yuan ($1,513).

The agency later told Faye that the university had changed its policy and would no longer accept medical certificates issued in China. Instead, she was required to obtain a certificate from a GP in Australia.

She then paid $45 out of pocket to obtain a medical certificate from a Melbourne GP and, with the agency's help, submitted the documents to the university. However, her application was rejected.

Why students seek outside help

Hongzhi Zhang, a senior lecturer at Monash University's Faculty of Education, who studied cultural perspectives in education, believes a lack of information is a primary reason students turn to commercial appeals agencies.

Universities generally provide students access to support and advice through their own services, but some students may not know those options are available.

Hongzhi Zhang, a senior lecturer at Monash University's Faculty of Education, says some students may distrust the support their universities offer and believe external organisations are better placed to represent their interests. Source: Supplied / Hongzhi Zhang

Zhang says some students may not trust the support their universities provide and may believe external organisations can better represent their interests.

He says students may also assume paying an outside organisation gives them a better chance at securing a favourable outcome.

"The internal support services are there to advocate for students and represent their interests. They can provide you with more accurate information, whereas external organisations may exaggerate the problem and make students even more anxious," he tells SBS Chinese.

Sometimes, students are looking for help in the wrong places. The first place they should turn to is the university, not outside agencies.

The price of an appeal

Sean Li is the founder of an education appeals agency based in Hangzhou, China. He graduated from RMIT University before completing a master's degree at Monash University.

He says his company was established about two years ago and currently assists between 30 and 50 students each month. His company charges around $2,000 for services related to academic misconduct cases.

Sean Li, the founder of an education appeal agency, says the industry aims to give students who have made mistakes a second chance. Source: Supplied

Li says they first help students determine whether their actions breached university rules before helping them prepare their appeal submissions.

We never help students fabricate anything. We don't make up facts for them either. If something didn't happen, then it didn't happen.

But he acknowledges questionable practices within the industry, including aggressive marketing, exaggerated claims about success rates, and in some cases, the use of fraudulent documents.

"Salespeople on the front end may sometimes over-promote the service when they're marketing it, and they may make excessive promises to clients about a particular outcome."

Li says he has also seen students obtain what were described as supporting documents from other agencies, some of which he believed were not genuine.

"If those documents are checked and found to be fake, the student could be in serious trouble. They could potentially be permanently expelled."

He rejects the suggestion that appeals agencies exploit the anxiety of international students.

He says the role of an appeals agency can be compared with the support universities themselves provide to students facing disciplinary processes.

We know students will make mistakes, and we're willing to give students another chance to continue their studies.

"The purpose of education shouldn't be for one failure to bring everything to an end. It should be about giving people who are willing to work hard a chance to keep moving forward."

A system under pressure

A TEQSA spokesperson told SBS Chinese: "TEQSA is aware that commercial academic cheating services continually evolve their strategies and services."

TEQSA published resources for students in November 2025 to help them prepare for and respond to academic misconduct processes.

"These resources support students to respond to allegations of academic misconduct without purchasing support from academic cheating services," the spokesperson said.

TEQSA said anyone who comes across advertisements for commercial academic cheating services or offers to provide access to assessment materials can report them to the agency.

Zhang says universities also have a responsibility to make their processes easier for international students to understand, particularly those from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds.

He suggests universities provide more multilingual services in addition to English, and include information about student support services when notifying students that they need to attend a hearing.

The emergence of these education appeals agencies is an opportunity for universities to reflect.

"If universities already have such comprehensive systems in place to support students, then why aren't students turning to you for help? Why are they going to external providers instead?"

Jha says universities also need to rethink how they design exams and assessments.

"If student assessment is no longer focused on rote memorisation, but instead on how knowledge is constructed, then these technologies can genuinely help students rather than being used for academic misconduct," she says.

She also recommends measures to detect Bluetooth signals and wearable devices during exams.

"There are some advanced smart gates available that can actually detect these devices when students are entering."

But she says there is a gap between rapidly evolving technology and the policies designed to regulate it.

Technology always takes a step and the policies follow it.

title: Rescuers race to find Australian hiker missing on remote Peruvian trail
text:
In brief Jordan Yap last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek.

Rescue crews completed their biggest day of search operations so far on Sunday morning (AEST).

Loved ones of a missing Australian trekker who was last seen nearly two weeks ago on a remote South American hiking trail are urging local authorities to help with the search.

A wide-scale sweep by a private rescue crew has so far failed to find any trace of 30-year-old Jordan Yap, who last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru's Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.

He was last seen near the start of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, regarded as a challenging, high-altitude route through the remote Andes.

Regarded as a very experienced hiker by friends and family, the Melbourne man failed to make contact on Wednesday, his estimated return date.

He also failed to check back into the Krusty Hostel in Huaraz, where his luggage remains stored, and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco on Thursday.

"It's really uncharacteristic of him to not have communicated at any point in his journey if he had the chance to," long-time friend Kevin Nguyen told the Australian Associated Press.

"It is a very popular trek, where you might have 200 to 300 hikers and guides per week during the busy season, so it is very uncharacteristic that no one's seen him since day one or day two."

The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.

Local mountain rescue organisation Socorro Andino Peruano has been hired by Yap's family to help with the search.

His loved ones hope the rescue group, which recently rescued a Canadian trekker from the same trail, can find him safe.

"Time is of the essence ... because ultimately, as much as we were saying he's been missing since the 23rd, he's had no contact with anyone since the 14th," Nguyen said.

Rescue crews completed their biggest day of search operations so far on Sunday morning (AEST), scouring various trails on the circuit to no avail.

"I know Jordan likes to orienteer and navigate and he's quite an adventurer himself, so I wouldn't be surprised if he tried an alternative route," Nguyen said.

Missing Australian hiker Jordan Yap (right), pictured with friend Kevin Nguyen during a previous hike of Mount Kosciuszko in Snowy Mountains. Source: Supplied, AAP / Kevin Nguyen

Yap had been planning the trek for more than a year and had recently bought a GPS watch to allow for offline maps to guide him on the hike.

"He was telling everyone about how he was ready to go on a big hike like this, (he was) really excited," Nguyen said.

He was last known to be wearing a white jacket, green sunshade sweater and grey pants.

The experienced trekker was believed to be carrying a 40-litre hiking bag, Durston dome tent and hiking poles.

Family and friends are urging the Australian government to work with Peruvian officials and local authorities to mobilise further resources in and around the rugged region.

The Australian embassy in Peru is helping his family.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

title: The cold drink stirring up a viral debate about professionalism
text:
In brief A recruiter in the US said Gen Z candidates are showing up to interviews with iced drinks and she perceives it as "too casual".

The take has proven divisive, with some agreeing and others viewing it as a dated idea of professionalism.

It's yet another debate dividing generations and the internet. At the heart of this one? Iced coffee in a job interview.

A recruiter's TikTok video has set off a viral online debate about whether it's appropriate to bring an iced coffee to an interview.

"My Gen Z candidates are showing up to their interviews with iced coffee, iced latte in hand," US-based recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen said in the video.

"It is perceived, from my opinion, my hiring standpoint, that when you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte that this interview is just like a stop on your list of errands on the day."

"It looks a little too casual to me," she added, advising candidates to finish their drinks before or after meeting with prospective employers.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While some commenters agreed that bringing an iced drink into a job interview was unprofessional and too informal, others argued it was an outdated and arbitrary way to judge a candidate.

"Are you expecting my whole day to revolve around a 30 min meeting?" one commenter wrote.

"As a millennial, can we please let go of the weird rules boomers and Gen X imposed on us? Interviews are stressful enough," said another.

"It's not about coffee it's about professionalism," another commented. "Surprised people aren't getting that."

Wehniainen later joked on LinkedIn that she had accidentally started a national debate and her comment section had become a battlefield.

She said she was "never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate".

"My point was simply about avoiding distractions."

An industry insider's take

Amy Slade-Symons has been a career coach for around 10 years and worked in talent recruitment and HR for more than a decade before that.

She told SBS News she personally wouldn't bring a coffee into a job interview, but it also shouldn't be a big deal if you do — as long as you're on time.

"It's just always is bad form if you turn up late, no matter what, and you're holding some form of drink in your hand," she said.

She noted, though, that she can't speak for everyone, and different hiring professionals have different biases.

But "if the candidate makes a great impression — skills, experience, motivation for the role, what they can bring — I think that eclipses most things", she added.

Government analysis suggests young people face an increasingly difficult path into the workforce, with the transition from education to employment becoming more complex and many entry-level roles ultimately going to more experienced candidates.

Australia's workforce is more generationally diverse than ever, with four generations working alongside one another.

With Generation Alpha beginning to enter the workforce in the coming years, that could soon become five.

That brings different communication and leadership styles, expectations around formality and workplace attire, and approaches to learning together in one place, Slade-Symons said.

She has seen those expectations change significantly over her own career.

"I've gone from wearing a suit, stockings, full face of makeup, through to going into the office wearing trainers and a nice frock and maybe a business jacket over the top if I'm having a formal meeting," she said.

"You interview people now, and I might be online wearing a hoodie because that's the environment that they work in, or wearing a T-shirt."

As workplace norms evolve, she said it's easy to look at younger generations and think: "In my day that was different."

When it comes to iced coffee, her advice is that it's probably not worth risking it, even if it feels silly.

"Get their focus on the conversation about your skills and experience and how wonderful you are."
