title: 'Can't beat it': Brisbane Lions celebrations roar on after Grand Final glory
text:
In brief The Brisbane Lions are continuing celebrations in Melbourne.

Fans revelled with the team at the Brunswick Street Oval.

Celebrations were ongoing on Sunday after the Brisbane Lions pulled off a three-peat in a nail-biting AFL Grand Final the day before.

The players revelled with fans at the Brunswick Street Oval in the Melbourne suburb of Fitzroy, the historic home of the Fitzroy Lions, which merged with the Brisbane Bears to form the Brisbane Lions in 1996.

Lions fan Den Wulf, clad head to toe in team merch and riding a tinsel-covered bike, told The Age newspaper he'd been a fan since the 80s when he lived in Fitzroy.

"You can’t describe it. I couldn’t sleep last night. It’s an awesome feeling. You can’t beat it," he said.

Brisbane coach Chris Fagan told fans he didn't have much of a voice left after Saturday night's celebrations, which ran late into the early hours of the morning at the Pullman Hotel.

"We had a pretty good celebration last night," he told the crowd.

"It wasn't the prettiest of grand finals and for large parts of it we looked like we probably weren't going to win the game.

Brisbane Lions head coach Chris Fagan celebrated with fans in Melbourne on Sunday. Source: AAP / Joel Carrett

"But this group's got amazing heart and amazing resilience but when they got 17 points up and played that Wharfie thing [a short sound and music Fremantle celebration called 'Wharfie Time'], our boys fired up and were able to play the best five minutes you'll ever see in a Grand Final.

'One more year' for Fagan

Chants of "one more year" started up when Fagan walked on stage at the family event in Fitzroy.

After completing his tenth season as coach, capped off with an incredible grand final triumph, Fagan is said to be considering ending his Lions career on a high.

The 65-year-old received louder applause than any of the players at Sunday's event.

"We love you Fagan," fans screamed out before he spoke.

Video of him partying on the shoulders of star Lions defender Harris Andrews has already gone viral.

Fagan had prepared his Lions for the Dockers' use of their in-game 'Wharfie Time' activation.

The Lions turned it to their advantage, scoring four goals in as many minutes.

All Lions players managed to make it to Brunswick St Oval, except for youngster Levi Ashcroft.

The 19-year-old got "a bit excited" in celebrating his second premiership in as many seasons in the AFL, according to teammate Ryan Lester.

title: Flood disaster declared in Bangkok after more than 300mm falls in monsoon deluge
text:
Key Points More than 300mm of rain has fallen on Bangkok in 48 hours, causing flood across the city.

A flood disaster was declared across the city, and the prime minister cut short a trip to London.

Bangkok authorities declared a flood disaster across the Thai capital on Saturday after almost 48 hours of heavy rain left homes, shops and roads waterlogged and residents wading through waist-deep water.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul cut short a trip to London to return home after more than 300mm of rain fell in some areas between Thursday afternoon and Saturday morning, according to officials.

"The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now," said Somkid Pheuk-ngam, 67, a vendor who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok.

"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now," she told AFP.

Bangkok is no stranger to wet weather, and September is the peak of the rainy season, but several residents said it felt worse than usual.

"I feel like in all the many years I've lived here, I've never encountered anything like this, where it rains continuously for days," said 63-year-old resident Anutin Meechamnan.

The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) declared a disaster across all 50 districts of the city, a move that grants local organisations special powers to act.

READ MORE Why scientists are collecting orangutan poo deep in the Borneo jungle

Bangkok governor Chadchart Sittipunt said on Saturday afternoon that the situation had "stabilised", adding: "If more rainwater doesn't fall in the area, it will be solved."

"If the rain stops, it is expected that it will take two to three days to drain the floodwater," he said in an update broadcast on social media.

Temporary shelters

Almost continuous rain since Thursday afternoon has swelled Bangkok's network of canals, sending murky water into surrounding homes, restaurants, shops and alleyways.

"Our problem is that the canals are full," Chadchart said.

"We are cooperating with nearby provinces and try to drain water out through other sides, minimising the amount that flows into Bangkok."

Bangkok is built on former marshland and rests about 1.5 metres above sea level.

READ MORE Two years on the run, these parents teach survival skills no child should need

The BMA said earlier that the city's pumping stations were operating at full capacity, drawing a combined 1,200 cubic metres per second.

AFP reporters saw residents wading or pushing their motorcycles through high waters in several districts of eastern Bangkok, while parked cars were partially submerged on one major road.

In Bang Bua district, a woman tried to salvage goods from her shop as the floodwaters rose to her thighs.

Khem Amnueilaph, an office worker who lives in Suan Luang district in eastern Bangkok, said the water in his neighbourhood was "higher than knee level".

"My house is new so it was elevated, but some old houses nearby the water have already flooded," the 36-year-old told AFP by telephone.

"I have food in my stock for two to three days, but I may have to wade through the floodwater for food later," he said, adding: "I have no idea how to get to work on Monday."

Some convenience stores were out of stock by lunchtime as residents raced to buy essentials.

Chadchart said at least 13 major roads were flooded but urged residents not to worry about potential food shortages, stressing: "The public doesn't have to be panicked."

He said around 980 people were staying in temporary shelters, while authorities had transferred 36 bedridden people to hospitals. The city has also prepared one million sandbags.

Despite hopes that the water will recede, Bangkok authorities said schools would close on Monday, while some officials have been asked to work from home.

September has been wetter than usual, according to figures from Bangkok's drainage and sewerage department.

The capital recorded 487mm of rain between 1 and 25 September compared to an average of almost 269mm for the same period from 1991 to 2020.

Scientists warn the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as the planet continues to warm due to fossil fuel emissions.

Flooding was also reported on Saturday across 21 provinces in Thailand, according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation, with more rain expected on Sunday.

Widespread deluges across the country in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.

title: Migrants are sending billions overseas. What does it mean for Australia's economy?
text:
In brief Remittances have become a contentious point in Australia's migration debate.

Critics argue they drain the Australian economy, while proponents say the provide a crucial lifeline to family abroad.

Remittances have become a talking point in Australia's migration debate.

Some anti-immigration activists argue remittances drain money from the Australian economy, while others say that view ignores migrants' economic contribution and the support these payments provide to families overseas.

So what's the real impact — both for the economy and for migrants and their families?

Mrinaal Datt, who moved to Australia from India four years ago and is the founder of Indian Women Abroad, regularly sends money back to India — often a few hundred dollars at a time.

She told SBS Examines that the remittances went towards her partner's parents' medical expenses.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"In Indian and a lot of South Asian cultures in general, they have a saying that you don't just marry a person, you marry the whole family," she said.

"It's not just you and your partner. It's your siblings, your parents, their parents. You can't think of not supporting your family. It's just not comprehensible to an average person who comes from India.

"It just feels like it's your duty as a child to support them through all their medical procedures."

A Money Transfer Australia report said $35 billion was sent from Australia as remittances in 2024, including nearly $7 billion to India.

"When someone earns that money in Australia, but remits part of that portion overseas, that portion is not being spent here," political commentator Jaimie Johnstone said in a recent social media post about the report.

"That money is not going to an Australian cafe or restaurant. It's not being spent with an Australian tradie, it's not being used to purchase Australian products, not in an Australian shop, not circulating within an Australian household.

"And if we're going to have a serious national conversation about immigration, surely capital flowing out of our domestic economy should be part of that conversation too."

But Ryan Edwards, an associate economics professor at the Australian National University, says we should be sceptical of these numbers.

"We don’t really measure money going out very well ... those numbers are actually much softer," he said.

Even if those estimates were correct, "that would still be under 1 per cent of our economy" and tax had already been paid on the income.

He noted the argument against remittances didn't account for the benefits migrants bring.

"The real counterfactual here is one of a migrant versus no migrant," he said.

"You take away that person, yes, you've stopped the money from flowing out, but you've also stopped all the jobs, the wages that they spend here, often on things that Australians are producing, and the tax that they've paid.

"We know that most migrants tend to be net positive fiscal contributors."

Muhammad Omair Ziaee is a technology and healthcare entrepreneur of Pakistani heritage. He sends money to his family and employees back home in Pakistan, but he says most of the money his businesses make is spent in Australia.

"If we compare to the money which we're sending over ... that's under 20 per cent of what we actually earn and what we spend over here," he said.

Remittances part of culture

Supriya Singh, an adjunct sociology professor at La Trobe University, said money is "one of the foremost ways" to show care in many cultures.

"If you come from China, you come from Vietnam, you come from any part of the Middle East, you come from the Pacific; sending money home is a way you tell your family that you belong, that you're thinking of them, that you care for them."

She said care was expressed differently across cultures.

"Across the world, it's the people who do not send money home that are in the minority," she said.

However, Singh said remittances can be used as a tool for financial abuse, noting the issue came up during Victoria's Royal Commission into Family Violence.

"When a person is using them not for care but for appropriation. If the parents demand too much of the child and the child does not have enough money for his or her own settlement expenses, then remittances can become a medium of abuse," she said.

Strain on already tight budget

Datt from Indian Women Abroad said remittances are a cultural practice but can strain already tight budgets.

"I think parents have to realise is that your child is not your retirement plan," she said.

"Everyone who comes abroad knows that it is really really hard when you're paying for the university fee. So many people are living paycheque to paycheque. It really is like a cultural thing. I actually hope things will change for the next generation."

She added her contributions to Australia outweighed the remittances back home.

"If you think about all the money that we spent, the flights that we paid, the income tax that we pay, our rentals, our mortgage now, I think we've spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in Australia," she said.

"The $200 or $400 is sent back home. That's nothing in comparison."

According to a World Bank estimate, global remittances to low and middle-income countries reached $924 billion in 2023, and continued to be "essential drivers of economic and human development".

title: US and China agree on 'super intelligence' label for AI, cut tariffs by $42 billion
text:
In brief The US and China agreed to cut tariffs on $42.6 billion worth of goods and establish a new trade council.

The two countries will also launch formal AI talks, including a channel to manage AI-related incidents.

The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on US$30 billion ($42.63 billion) of goods and launch a dialogue on AI, both countries said following President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington.

The tariff reductions would apply to US exports such as agricultural goods, wood, and cosmetics, as well as US imports, including small appliances, toys, and decorations, a White House statement said on Friday, local time.

"The two countries reached consensus on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction," the White House said.

The three-day summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump, which ended on Friday, showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs. Xi has since landed in Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.

The two sides also agreed to establish a trade council and to extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the Chinese foreign ministry said.

title: Jane Hume says 'we're missing the point' on OpenAI Medicare breach
text:
In brief Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has criticised the government's response to the OpenAI Medicare breach.

It comes after the government suggested taking legal action against the US-based ChatGPT developer over the incident.

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has accused the federal government of "missing the point" in its response to the OpenAI Medicare breach, arguing the incident exposed serious gaps in Australia's cyber defences.

The government is examining whether those involved in the breach could be prosecuted under existing Australian law.

Environment Minister Murray Watt said a task force investigating the incident was seeking advice on what action was possible under current laws and whether changes were needed to deal with similar incidents in the future.

Speaking on ABC's Insiders on Sunday, Hume said the "real alarm bell" was that the government only became aware of the hack because OpenAI disclosed it.

"I'm not entirely sure who they're going to put into cuffs," she said. "I think we're missing the point here."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"If they hadn't of told us that there was a breach, would we have known about it at all? That demonstrates that our cyber defences, particularly for [Services Australia], was woefully inadequate."

She questioned whether OpenAI was at fault, adding, "the idea that we would only check an inbox once a day when that inbox is specifically set up to identify cybersecurity breaches is mind-boggling".

Her comments follow Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's revelation this week that an agent linked to OpenAI, the California-based developer of ChatGPT, gained unauthorised access to Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

Both the government and OpenAI have said no personal information was accessed during the breach, but it has raised broader concerns, including over the time it took to report it and who is accountable.

The 18 June incident was reported to Services Australia by OpenAI on 10 September, when the company emailed a Services Australia inbox.

Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said that inbox is typically used by researchers to alert the government agency to possible vulnerabilities in its systems, and is only checked once a day.

She said the email was discovered the next day and escalated on 15 September after checks to determine it was legitimate.

She said she was notified on 17 September. Albanese disclosed it publicly on 24 September.

PM says incident was not isolated

There have been dozens of cases of artificial intelligence agents wrongfully accessing classified information beyond Australia's Medicare hack, Albanese said on Saturday.

But he said he wasn't aware of them before revealing the unauthorised OpenAI infiltration of the Medicare Statistics Reporting portal while in New York on Thursday.

"At the time we made our announcement ... we weren't aware of other occurrences," the prime minister told reporters on the tarmac at Sydney airport.

"We were acting purely in our national interest."

Albanese returned to Australia after a week in the US, where he addressed the United Nations General Assembly on the international need to rein in AI.

He now says news that rogue AI agents hacked into US government websites is further proof of that need.

Autonomous agents are now known to have infiltrated US university and commerce department sites, as well as the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

"We now know it wasn't just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation," Albanese said.

"What this does is confirm that approach of making sure that it needs to be an appropriate national response, as well as an international response to make sure that humans are in charge of this new and emerging technology."

Albanese said it was up to OpenAI to state why multiple breaches occurred.

Albanese spoke with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman by phone while in New York, with the tech boss admitting the company had not done enough.

An OpenAI spokesperson said, “Yesterday we announced we've paused training our most capable models and will resume training them only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards and alignment improvements in place, which we are working on now."

Australia is among more than 20 countries that signed a joint statement calling for cooperation to establish global AI standards and ensure human control.

However, US President Donald Trump used a speech at the UN to lash out at calls to put the brakes on AI.

title: Emma's relationship ended. Now, she's caught in Australia's $2bn debt battle
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

This article contains references to family and domestic violence.

When Emma's relationship ended, the financial uncertainty didn't.

She says her former partner's child support payments became inconsistent, leaving her struggling to rely on the money she was entitled to. It forced her to rethink how she could protect herself and her child.

"I couldn't rely on the payments coming through," Emma tells SBS News.

There were elements of domestic violence, emotional abuse and coercive control behaviours.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

SBS News has withheld her surname for privacy reasons.

In a bid to protect herself and her child, Emma switched to Agency Collect, the government's Child Support Scheme (CSS), where Services Australia collects payments on behalf of separated parents.

For 18 months, Emma was receiving the child support she was entitled to — until the payments stopped.

She says her former partner took advantage of a "loophole" in the system and registered themselves as "self-employed" to avoid paying the amount she says was owed.

As of March 2026, almost $2 billion in child support debt was owed by parents using Agency Collect.

As of March 2026, outstanding child support debt among parents using Agency Collect stood at almost $2 billion. Source: iStockphoto / Tolikoff Photography/Getty Images/iStockphoto

A Department of Social Services (DSS) spokesperson told SBS News: "The amount of unpaid child support in this country is utterly unacceptable ... This is parents robbing their children of the support they need and in many cases leaving them to live in poverty."

But that figure only captures debt recorded through Agency Collect. It does not include unpaid child support under private arrangements between parents, meaning the full scale of the problem is unknown.

Emma's experience raises questions about how Australia's child support system responds when payments stop and what happens when financial control continues after a relationship ends.

How Australia's Child Support Scheme works

The CSS was introduced in 1988. It was designed to create a national system for assessing and collecting child support, with the aim of ensuring separated parents contributed financially to the cost of raising their children.

The scheme initially relied heavily on compulsory collection, including through wage withholding, where child support could be deducted from a person's salary.

However, by the mid-1990s, the scheme was reformed, giving parents greater choice over how their child support was collected.

Professor Kay Cook is an associate dean of research at Swinburne University of Technology, who specialises in child support policy. She says the reforms reflected a view within the government at the time that the system was "too onerous" on fathers.

They gave parents more choice, and it was all done under the rhetoric of making it easier and fairer ... but it returned all the power to the fathers.

Cook argues the changes shifted greater responsibility for managing child support onto parents, while government policy at the time emphasised giving separated parents more choice and flexibility in how payments were arranged.

For separated parents, there are two main routes for child support payment.

The first is Private Collect, a personal agreement in which payments are handled by the two parents without Services Australia collecting or monitoring.

Child support can be handled privately between separated parents or collected and managed by Services Australia through Agency Collect. Source: Moment RF / krisanapong detraphiphat/Getty Images

The second is Agency Collect, which is organised and overseen by the government through Services Australia.

There are 1.2 million Australians who have a child support arrangement — with 590,300 actively using Agency Collect.

The $1.99 billion owed by parents using Agency Collect does not capture those with Private Collect arrangements.

SBS News understands there are currently 229,355 non-paying parents — and only 59.4 per cent of them have an active repayment arrangement.

"We have no idea what is happening in the other half," Cook says, referring to Private Collect arrangements.

She believes the amount would be much higher.

Does the debt signal a bigger issue?

The debt is a result of an "underpayment of the amount that is meant to be paid in child support", according to Cook.

She says it most commonly occurs when the paying parent declares they are self-employed or "choose to pay or not pay when they want".

"People manipulate how much they pay, through working cash-in-hand jobs, or keeping their own business," she says.

They make their taxable income look really small.

Cook says there are little to no repercussions, describing Services Australia as a "toothless tiger".

In 2025, the Commonwealth Ombudsman investigated complaints about Services Australia's response to withheld payments and what it described as the "weaponisation" of child support.

The investigation found that Services Australia was "not doing enough to identify and respond to financial abuse through the Child Support program" and lacked "policies, strategies and training to be able to proactively identify, monitor and respond to cases of financial abuse".

A 2025 Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation found Services Australia was not doing enough to identify and respond to financial abuse through the Child Support program. Source: Moment RF / Kseniya Ovchinnikova/Getty Images

These findings prompted an Australian National Audit Office audit of Services Australia's child support debt-recovery enforcement powers. The findings are scheduled to be tabled in November 2026.

It's estimated that almost 100,000 parents using Agency Collect have experienced or are at risk of experiencing family or domestic violence.

Cook says the CSS operates under "the assumption that parents are equally bargaining and making decisions".

"But, in family violence ... when a perpetrator can't physically control you anymore, the number one tool they have left is to financially control you."

Adrianne Walters, executive director of Women's Legal Services Australia, says the "deliberate nonpayment of child support is economic abuse".

"It takes food off the table, destabilises households, and it punishes children in order to control their mothers," she tells SBS News.

The body recently surveyed 540 separated mothers, finding that 80 per cent reported experiencing financial abuse via the CSS.

Walters says the body regularly witnesses "women exhausted by the process".

"Years of underpayment and mounting debts, and the stress of other legal processes while the child support system asks them to keep pursuing a person they might be frightened of. Many simply give up," she says.

While the child support system has provisions intended to protect people experiencing family and domestic violence, Cook says they fail to account for the nuances of financial abuse.

"You have to prove it, and the system knows what to do with physical abuse, but it's not very good at recognising coercive control and financial abuse," she says.

[The CSS] is compelling women to be tied administratively to their abuser for decades.

"Instead, lots of women are just going to Private Collect and aren't collecting anything."

Do the new reforms actually fix the problems?

In the 2026-27 federal budget, the government announced a landmark $182.6 million investment over four years to reform the CSS.

The reforms include removing the requirement for certain personal financial information to be automatically shared with the other parent, increasing discretionary powers to limit harassment and harm between parents, expanding wage withholding and introducing a new Collection Arrangement Guidance Tool for new parents entering the CSS.

The government will also "strengthen data sharing" between Services Australia and the Australian Taxation Office and "prosecute people who don't lodge their tax returns to avoid their child support responsibilities".

From 1 July 2027, the government plans to automate the issuing of Departure Prohibition Orders (DPOs), a legal tool used by authorities to prevent people with significant unpaid debts from leaving the country.

That will include automatically issuing DPOs to some parents with child support debt of at least $10,000 who have travelled overseas more than once in the previous two years.

"We believe that if you can afford an overseas trip, then you can afford your child support," a DSS spokesperson told SBS News in a statement.

In the 2025-26 financial year, 672 DPOs were issued, according to the government. It expects the reforms to result in an extra 3,000 DPOs being issued in the first year.

Reforms will be legislated "progressively, with the first tranche to be introduced in parliament in the coming weeks", the spokesperson said.

Cook says the changes are "underwhelming" but are the "beginning of system change".

Walters noted that while they're the "most significant action taken against systems abuse in recent history", they fall short and do not fully address the experiences of parents in Private Collect arrangements.

She hopes to see the changes implemented with the safety of victim-survivors as a priority, and stronger access to free, specialist legal support for women to navigate the system safely.

"We need action to stop perpetrators from forcing women into Private Collect arrangements — like making Agency Collect the default arrangement until certain safeguards are met," Walters says.

"These actions must be accompanied by stronger accountability for deliberate non-payment ... better options for reviewing and enforcing Private Collect arrangements, so non-payment doesn't disappear from view."

The child support system means Emma will remain financially connected to her ex-partner until their child is at least 18. Credit: Christopher Hopefitch/Getty Images

Like many parents using the CSS, Emma will remain connected to her ex-partner until their child is at least 18 years old.

Believing the insecurity of payments kept her in the "cycle of abuse", she's worked hard to no longer be reliant on child support.

It came with significant sacrifice.

Sometimes you might have to ask people, your family, for help. You have to cancel things for yourself that might help your mental health.

"You might have to find housing in a non-ideal area because it's all you can afford, and you might have to work and juggle more.

"It's just part of the sacrifices you make as a parent — you put your child first."

title: After a one-night stand, this comedian was told he’d be a dad. But not all was as it seemed
text:
Comedian Simon Taylor got sick of being asked why he doesn’t have a podcast, so made a sitcom about podcasters.

Comedian Simon Taylor received a Facebook message after a casual encounter. It changed his life – just not in the way he imagined.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Among the people inadvertently promoting Simon Taylor’s new sitcom The Sonny Disposition – a satire about the chaotic, ego-driven world of podcasting – are Kyle Sandilands, Karl Stefanovic and Anthony Albanese. “The timing is perfect,” says the comedian, who created the series with Josh Samuels. “Every day, someone in my team is messaging me going, ‘Kyle Sandilands just started a podcast! Karl’s in the news for an episode about right-wing extremists!’ And then Albo got himself in trouble [over the so-called melon-gate affair].” But the idea for The Sonny Disposition occurred well before these headline-grabbing incidents. “It actually came from me not wanting to do a podcast,” says the 38-year-old, who was hired as a writer for The Tonight Show with Jay Leno at 24 before becoming the first Australian stand-up to perform on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. “Everyone’s like, ‘You’re a comedian; where’s your podcast?’ But I’m so sick of them. There are so many already, and I don’t know what I’d be offering that’s different. So I’m offering this instead – a sitcom about podcasters.” What fascinates Taylor is the medium’s “Wild West” aspect, and the performative authenticity of many hosts. “As a journalist, you have to follow ethical guidelines,” he says. “But as a podcaster, you can reach an audience without any of those pesky ethics. You get to be the CEO as well as the face of the show. You’re a gunslinger; you’ll do anything to beat the other guy’s ratings and win over the algorithm.”

Advertisement

Worst habit? Drinking coffee after 9pm. I always feel like I need to get a bit more work done before bed so I’ll have a coffee, work until 1am and then sleep better knowing I’ve ticked off a few things. It’s a terrible health habit but my mum’s side of the family is Italian, and my grandparents would always have coffee after dinner, so maybe I have enough Italian DNA to handle it. Greatest fear? I have nightmares about my wife ghosting me. I’ll wake up and go, “You left me again, you blocked me.” But my wife and I have a good rule. We don’t say, “You did this in my dreams”; I’ll say, “Dream Lucy did this”, and she’ll say, “Dream Simon did this.” If I were to psychoanalyse myself, I’d guess it’s about losing what makes me happiest: being at home with my family. Taylor (centre) with the cast of The Sonny Disposition. The line that stayed with you? There’s variations of this line going around but my friend, Philip Escoffey, a magician from the UK, distilled it into a nice quote: “Luck gets you through the door but hard work determines how long you stay there.” In a career like this, you never know when you’ll get a break. I’ve had lucky moments, but to stay in the game I have to keep writing jokes so I’m always ready. I know people who make a living from social media, but I’m not jealous of them because they’re constantly posting and checking their numbers, even when they’re talking to their friends. If I did that, it would change my relationship with my family. I just want to get home, put my phone on “do not disturb” and engage with my kids.

Advertisement

Biggest regret? Not embracing the comedy community earlier. When I started, I thought I was a lone wolf. It took me 10 years to realise that this is a team sport in many ways. We’re a collective of comedians who look after each other. Related Article Take 7 How Aja Monet traded poetry slams for Grammy nods Tell us about your turning point … I wrote a book about this. In my 20s, I had a one-night stand – and then I was told I was going to be a dad. I got a Facebook message, then a phone call. I was 27, very career-focused and on the road a lot. That’s when the world changed for me. I was really emotional; I was excited but also worried because I didn’t really know the woman. Then I was told, “No, it might be another guy.” So it was nine months of me waiting to see whether it was me or this other guy. When I did the test, I found out I wasn’t the dad. But it was a turning point for me in the dating world because it made me realise that I wanted to be a father. Until then, I felt lacking, like there was something missing. This allowed me to be upfront and say, “I want marriage and kids.”

MoneySuper & retirementPension Opinion The hidden cost of downsizing: How your home’s sale can hit your pension Rachel Lane Money contributor September 29, 2026 — 3:00pm

September 29, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Downsizing can free up equity to invest or spend. But for retirees receiving the age pension that can be a problem as you may be converting an exempt asset into an assessable one. New data from over-50s developer GemLife shows that, of 1474 purchasers across 12 communities, the average equity release was $254,098 when downsizing into a land lease community. Downsizing your home can mean downsizing your pension. A Stockland land lease community. That $254,000 can boost your savings, buy a new car, caravan or boat or help out the kids but it can also reduce your pension and other benefits. For pensioners, the magic numbers are $333,000 if you’re single and $499,000 for couples. These are the asset test thresholds. Once your assessable assets exceed the threshold, your pension reduces by $3 a fortnight for every $1000 above the threshold.

Advertisement

Put simply you lose $7800 per year of pension for every $100,000 of assets over the threshold. Related Article Opinion

Aged care The alarming reason one in three seniors are giving up aged care Rachel Lane Money contributor So what does releasing $254,000 actually mean? Well, it depends on what you start with. A single person starting with $50,000 in assets would have $304,000. They would be below the $333,000 threshold, so there would be no reduction under the assets test. If they started with $250,000, their assets would rise to $504,000, which is $171,000 over the threshold, their pension would be reduced by $513 a fortnight, or $13,338 a year.

Advertisement

And if they started with $500,000 they would have $754,000 after they downsize, that’s over the cut-off of $745,750, so their pension would be lost. Couples can have more. A couple starting with $200,000 would have $454,000 after they move, and still be below the $499,000 assets threshold. The question isn’t just how much equity can you unlock: it’s how much retirement income you will have left once you do. If they started with $500,000 they would have $754,000 which is $255,000 above the threshold, reducing their pension by about $765 a fortnight, or $19,890 a year, under the assets test. And if they start with $867,000 or more the move would push them above the $1.121 million cut-off and their pension would be lost.

Advertisement

These examples are deliberately looking only at the assets test. How you invest or spend matters. If you invest it, the income can help offset any pension reduction, but the deemed income will be used to calculate your pension under the income test. Related Article Ask an expert ‘Shock and disbelief’: The pitfalls of buying property with your children If you spend it on a boat, car or caravan, those assets still count under the assets test but only at market value. It’s important to understand that your pension will be paid based on whichever test, income or assets, produces the lowest pension. Downsizing your home can mean downsizing your pension, that doesn’t automatically make it a bad decision. You need to understand how much equity you will release, what you will do with it and how it will affect your pension and other benefits. In a land lease community getting at least some pension can take on extra importance because the site fees qualify as rent for rent assistance, potentially adding up to $5819 a year (single) or $5486 (couple) on top of your pension.

The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to a 15-year high to combat stubborn inflation and has not ruled out further hikes despite rising unemployment, falling house prices and sluggish economic growth. The bank’s monetary policy board decided unanimously to raise its benchmark cash rate by 0.25 of a percentage point to 4.6 per cent on Tuesday, adding more than $90 a month to repayments on a typical $600,000 mortgage with 25 years remaining. RBA governor Michele Bullock. Louie Douvis The increase means Australia now has one of the highest official interest rates set by a central bank among western economies, surpassing the US (where official rates are 4 per cent) and UK (3.75 per cent). In a statement, the RBA board left the door open for additional interest rate increases, saying it will “continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed”.

Advertisement

The board said previously flagged “upside risks” to inflation were now materialising, citing the fallout from war in the Middle East, the AI boom and prices surges across the economy. “There have been further disruptions to global oil supply and recent data suggest that growth and inflation in Australia have been higher than expected,” the board said. “Higher fuel prices have partially been passed through to prices of other goods and services. This inflation impulse is in addition to the effect of capacity pressures in the economy.” The board acknowledged the housing downturn, noting that “weak productivity growth continues to constrain potential growth and there are uncertainties about the economic effects of the downturn in the housing market”.

Advertisement

The last time Australia’s cash rate was above 4.5 per cent was October 2011. However, the amount of outstanding mortgage debt has more than doubled since then. The total value of residential mortgages in 2011 was $1.05 trillion, but that has since climbed to $2.51 trillion, according the Australian Prudential Regulatory Authority. The RBA has now lifted interest rates by 1 percentage point over four separate increases this year in a bid to reduce inflation. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6 per cent in 15-year high; OpenAI apologises for Medicare data breach Price pressures have been stoked by elevated fuel prices caused by the Middle East conflict, which has dragged on since February and continues to disrupt global oil supplies. Average petrol prices in Australia have risen well above the $2-a-litre mark in the past month, putting pressure on the Albanese government to revive the fuel excise cuts that subsidised the cost for four months from April through July this year, and spurring other price rises as firms pass on this cost. The RBA’s decision also follows a volatile period of international bond markets as global interest rates climb to two decade highs amid concerns about higher inflation and geopolitical risk.

Advertisement

Australia’s inflation rate is currently 3.5 per cent and has been above the RBA’s target band of 2 to 3 per cent for much of the past five years. Reserve Bank officials have repeatedly expressed concern that expectations of elevated inflation have becoming more entrenched among business and consumers. Last month the unemployment rate reached 4.6 per cent, the highest rate in nearly five years, but the deterioration in the labour market was not enough to deter the RBA from lifting interest rates. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock warned last week the jobless rate may need to rise as high as 5 per cent to ease pressure on inflation. Higher interest rates will hit a housing market already weakened by higher borrowing costs and federal tax changes. Figures released in early September by property analytics firm Cotality showed house values have fallen for five consecutive months. The Australian stock market was down very slightly after the Reserve Bank of Australia met expectations and raised the cash rate to 4.6 per cent, up 25 basis points, on Tuesday afternoon.

Advertisement

The ASX 200 index had been trading at 8690, up about 0.11 per cent for the day, at 2.20pm AEST. At 2.32pm, just after the rates call, the index was at 8675, down 0.04 per cent. The central bank’s decision had been widely expected among market watchers and investors. Ahead of the decision, AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said he expected the bank to continue warning of further rate hikes, but that the tone may shift later in the year. “After more than five years of inflation being above target, threatening RBA credibility, it does not have the luxury of continuing to ‘wait and assess’,” he said. “By the time it gets to the November meeting, there is likely to be more evidence of a cooling economy, falling home prices, a softer jobs market and rising recession risks – so we don’t think a second hike let alone a third will be necessary.”

Advertisement

Oliver said rate hikes and higher petrol prices have raised the additional monthly costs for an average household by $530 a month since January for those with a mortgage and petrol car, which he said was “quite a hit”. The economy grew by 2.1 per cent last financial year, but gross domestic product per person rose by a more subdued 0.7 per cent. The Reserve Bank is forecasting growth the slow to 1.5 per cent in the year to June 2027. Inflation peaked at nearly 8 per cent at the end of 2022 but then fell back to the RBA’s 2–3 per cent target range for a period in 2024 and 2025. However, it picked up in the second half of 2025 and has remained above the target since. Bullock and other RBA officials have said repeatedly the bank is focused on getting inflation back into the 2-3 per cent band. title: Accelerate grabs full control of Pilbara manganese play
text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Accelerate grabs full control of Pilbara manganese play Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 29, 2026 — 2:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Accelerate Resources has grabbed full control of its Woodie Woodie North manganese project 260 kilometres east of Port Hedland in WA’s East Pilbara region in a savvy move that clears the decks of all legacy payments and royalties ahead of a significant drilling campaign planned for next month. The company has executed two binding, share-only agreements that deliver 100 per cent of the 432-square-kilometre tenure. The deals simplify a previously complex ownership structure and remove any future milestone payments, which could otherwise have potentially cost the company up to $2 million in cash and 20 million shares. Outcropping manganese at Accelerate Resources’ Woodie Woodie North project, just 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine in the Pilbara. In the first transaction, Accelerate will acquire full title to two key exploration licences by issuing 25 million shares to subsidiaries of First Development Resources. The shares will be subject to a 12-month voluntary escrow period. Previously, the company held only the manganese and iron ore rights over the tenements under a 2021 option. The deal now gives it outright ownership and extinguishes all remaining claims, including milestone payments and royalties.

Advertisement

‘All manganese we discover and develop at Woodie Woodie North will now belong solely to Accelerate shareholders.’ Accelerate Resources chief executive officer and managing director Luke Meter A second transaction involves Accelerate issuing 30 million shares to a group of seven unrelated vendors to terminate all legacy agreements across the wider project. The move scrubs all future milestone payments, deferred consideration, royalties and reversionary rights tied to resource definition and development. The company says the two scrip-based deals mean no cash will leave its coffers for the acquisitions, leaving it well-funded for its upcoming exploration push. Key to the consolidation is that Accelerate now stands to capture 100 per cent of the upside from any future discovery, resource upgrade or development at Woodie Woodie North. Management says the simplified structure will also better support any potential funding, offtake or partnering discussions down the track. Accelerate Resources chief executive officer and managing director Luke Meter said: “This is a decisive simplification of the Woodie Woodie North ownership structure. On Completion, we will own the Area 42 corridor outright and every remaining milestone payment across the project will be extinguished, with no cash leaving the Company. From that point, all manganese we discover and develop at WWN will belong solely to Accelerate shareholders.”

Advertisement

The Woodie Woodie North project sits 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine. The company has already carved out a maiden inferred mineral resource of 1.2 million tonnes grading 19.1 per cent manganese, alongside an exploration target of between 5.3 and 10.7 million tonnes at grades of 10 to 19 per cent manganese. Being on the doorstep of a major, multi-decade mining operation is an enviable position for any explorer. Perhaps more importantly though, the at-surface geology doesn’t respect tenement boundaries, with Accelerate saying it appears to be sitting on a significant extension of the same mineralised system that has made its neighbour a globally significant producer. With the ownership structure now cleaned up, the company is turning its focus to the drill bit. Scheduled for October, maiden drilling at the project’s Gingarrigan prospect follows recent mapping that identified more than 200 manganese outcrops across it and the nearby El Largo area, outlining a combined manganese footprint of almost 10 hectares. Rock chip sampling from the outcrops returned high-grade results of up to an impressive 59.4 per cent manganese. The upcoming 3000-metre reverse-circulation program will test the continuity of the surface mineralisation at depth and along strike, with management eyeing the potential to add a second resource area to the project.

Advertisement

Additionally, rock chip sampling from the company’s newly defined Rancor and Wampa prospects has returned grades as high as 58.4 per cent manganese, with a slew of other impressive hits including 57.6 per cent and 55.6 per cent manganese. For context, Australia’s two major operating mines at Woodie Woodie and Groote Eylandt run resource grades of 45.5per cent and 43.6 per cent manganese, respectively. The outcropping grades look bang on for direct-shipping ore (DSO). DSO is the holy grail for bulk commodity miners, meaning the ore is high-grade enough to be dug up and shipped directly to customers with minimal processing, dramatically slashing both capital and operating costs. Accelerate’s focus on manganese is part of a dual-pronged strategy, which also includes the Balagundi gold project near Kalgoorlie. In a nod to its two key commodities, the company is planning to rebrand as “Mango Metals”, a combination of the words manganese and gold. For now, however, all eyes are on the manganese. Having tidied up its ownership and removed the burden of legacy payments, Accelerate has a clear run at its Pilbara project. If the upcoming drilling at Gingarrigan can convert those high-grade surface rocks into a significant discovery, taking full control of the project will look like a very shrewd piece of business indeed. title: How Europe’s abandoned villages are being transformed
text:
Advertisement

InspirationEurope How Europe’s abandoned villages are being transformed Chrissie McClatchie Updated September 29, 2026 — 2:14pm ,first published September 29, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Tuscan resort of Castelfalfi is at maximum capacity for its annual Spring Festival in late March – quite literally; it’s a sell-out. In December, 30,000 people came for its Christmas market, so management made the smart decision to ticket this weekend event, while keeping it free for locals. Even so, it still seems like every family in the Pisa-Siena-Florence triangle is making an appearance at some point over the two-day program, if the line of parked cars lining every access road to the hilltop village is anything to go by. Visitors descend on Castelfalfi for the annual spring festival in late March. As hotel guests, my 10-year-old daughter, Lottie, and I need only to flash our room key and we’re ushered straight past the security fence, where an explosion of music from competing loudspeakers awaits. Some stallholders – selling everything from potted flowers to truffle paste and lots of pretty handmade jewellery (including a lemon pendant necklace blown from Murano glass that’s calling my name) – look increasingly fatigued by the mash-up of Britney Spears and ABBA blasting through the air from different directions.

Advertisement

I, however, am completely swept up in the buzz, singing along while sipping a Paloma spritz poured from one of the food trucks. In classic pre-teen fashion, Lottie – deep in her own culinary heaven thanks to a bombolone (doughnut) filled with Kinder chocolate – keeps her distance from her ever-embarrassing mother. Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. Via Castelfalfi Castello and Via Castelfalfi haven’t always been so lively. In fact, for most of the late 20th century, the two streets that made up this borgo were silent. In a copy and paste of thousands of medieval settlements across Italy, the hillcrest village had emptied; the last of its residents lured to the big smoke and the opportunities it offered in the 1950s. Resort life in the countryside ... Castelfalfi’s pool. Junior suite at Castelfalfi … the property has secured two Michelin Keys and a Forbes five-star rating. The buttercream-toned huddle of stone buildings overlooking the Valdera – one of Tuscany’s lesser-known patches, yet only 45 minutes from both Pisa and San Gimignano – stood tall but forgotten, mementos of a bygone era when these valleys hummed with rural life.

Advertisement

Nearly two decades ago, German tourism group TUI acquired the entire village and its surrounding estate and took the first steps in transforming it into a high-end eco-resort. In 2021, it was sold to Indian-Indonesian billionaire Sri Prakash Lohia. The new owner has raised the bar. Among Castelfalfi’s current accolades are two Michelin Keys and a Forbes Travel Guide five-star rating, no doubt hooked on features such as a signature suite designed by Stefano Ricci inside the village’s 14th-century castle. En suite in the Stefano Ricci-designed La Rocca suite. Across the estate’s 1090 hectares, guests can book on-site activities ranging from truffle hunting and wine tasting to pizza making, lake fishing, e-bike touring and a night jeep safari. A sleeping beauty awakened, Castelfalfi’s fairytale is part of a growing hospitality trend that’s breathing new life into Europe’s abandoned hamlets and villages.

Advertisement

Many of these villages-turned-hotels fall under the concept of albergo diffuso, Italian for scattered hotels. The term is a nod to the typical character of these properties: rooms spread across multiple buildings in a village, with guests navigating cobblestone streets and covered alleyways instead of internal staircases and lifts to access communal areas such as breakfast rooms, reception desks and restaurants. Castelfalfi’s dining options include a sweet gelateria and a delicatessen straining under the weight of different styles of pecorino cheese, alongside a cosy pizzeria tucked along its main streets. Meals are accompanied by the estate’s olive oils (the rosemary-infused variety paired with freshly baked focaccia is a meal in itself), and attentive waitstaff top up my glass with elegant house wines. One of several dining options within the restored historical Castelfalfi Borgo village complex. Not all reborn villages come with Castelfalfi’s luxury trimmings – or price tag. Some of the most memorable reveal themselves only after dedicated internet sleuthing. That’s how another Italian spot, Colletta di Castelbianco, appeared on my radar more than a decade ago. Near the French border in Liguria, the village was severely damaged in an 1887 earthquake. Inhabitants started to trickle away, and by the 1970s, the population was a mere five people. In the 1980s, a group of local entrepreneurs banded together to revitalise it, emphasising original materials and techniques in the rebuild. Ahead of its time – and certainly pre the global pandemic remote work boom – the project was imagined as a “teleworking” community, although now it has a definite out-of-office vibe.

Advertisement

Colletta di Castelbianco was planned as a “teleworking” community before the COVID remote work boom. The hamlet appears glued among thick vegetation to the slopes of the unspoilt Pennavaira valley, about 20 minutes inland from the seaside resort of Albenga. Its silhouette resembles a cluster of Greek Island homes, only with flat-roofed buildings fashioned from slate grey stones rather than whitewashed walls. There’s nothing but nature’s greens for company, which I admire while floating in a lap pool built into the terraced landscape. A casual, vine-covered bar and bistro beckons for late afternoon aperitivo that drifts into dinner. The preserved medieval stone architecture of Colletta di Castelbianco. Tucked up in the northern reaches of France’s vine-speckled Languedoc region, Village Castigno is a scattered hotel in the village of Assignan that’s long been on my travel wish-list, too. While never abandoned, Assignan’s population had dwindled to less than 200, and the village’s demographics were steadily ageing when Belgian couple Marc and Tine Verstraete purchased and restored the nearby 12th-century chateau Castigno in 2007.

Advertisement

Late last year, when road-tripping across France’s Mediterranean arc with my sister and younger daughter, I thought I’d stumbled upon a savvy hack. Why pay €300-plus for a family room at the hotel when I could book a privately owned house in the village – with an “excellent 9.0 rating” on booking.com – for €77, instead? With the savings, I reasoned, we could splash out on dinner at Castigno’s acclaimed Thai restaurant, inside a spacious village house, and return as external guests for breakfast – coming out more or less even. Apart from where we slept, our stay would revolve around Castigno’s facilities. Check-in with our friendly host is smooth and our cottage home, called La Maison De Blanche Neige (Snow White’s House) for the evening is, on first impressions, cute if not a little musty. We don’t linger, keen to reach Chateau Castigno’s tasting room before it closes for the day at 5pm. Castigno’s acclaimed Thai restaurant, Le Thai de Castigno. Inside an impressive cork-wrapped structure shaped like a wine bottle when viewed from above, our cellar host shares the backstory: when the Verstraetes acquired the chateau and the surrounding vineyards, their intention was simply to make wines to enjoy with friends in their new home. Opportunity soon came knocking. Not only did they snap up 150 hectares of land surrounding the chateau, but also derelict properties in the village at their doorstep. Today, guests lodge in one of 21 rooms in apartments and standalone houses, temporary neighbours alongside Assignan’s permanent population of 160.

Advertisement

Related Article Travel tips The world’s 10 most charming villages (plus five in Australia) As we swill and swirl the vineyard’s fresh, juicy sparkling rosé, I mention where we’re staying. Our host nearly spits out his wine: it turns out that Snow White’s House doubles as a “love room”, available for short-stay rendezvous of the “romantic” kind – explaining the hooks on the ceiling in the main bedroom. We dissolve into laughter, the lesson swiftly learnt to book within the official scattered hotels themselves. Yet, our adventure makes for a great story when we return, and is one additional tale to add to the countless layers of history these old stone villages across the continent hold. THE DETAILS STAY

TechnologyAI ‘We are sorry’: OpenAI apologises for Medicare hack David Swan Updated September 29, 2026 — 2:06pm ,first published 11:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

OpenAI has apologised to Australians after revealing its AI model took credentials and internal files from a Medicare portal and attempted to breach NSW and Victorian government systems. In a blog post on Tuesday, titled “How we will do better for Australia”, the company said an experimental model found a way into Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service in June. Once inside, it “ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, and wrote files”. The model also reviewed the service’s technical system information and source code. Sam Altman’s OpenAI has published fresh details on how its agents breached a Medicare website. Bloomberg “We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said. “We also should have handled our response better.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday he had a “direct but constructive discussion” with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman last week. On Monday, he was briefed in Canberra on the work of the government’s taskforce investigating the incident.

Advertisement

“OpenAI have been very constructive and open in engaging in that process, and I welcome that,” Albanese said. He said Anthropic had also engaged constructively. OpenAI detailed how the hacks unfolded and pledged to make changes. In the lengthy post, it said it has now blocked live internet access in its research environments, and has paused training and evaluation involving tool use for its most capable models. It will set up a taskforce including independent Australian experts to recommend how AI developers and governments should detect and disclose incidents, with a report due by the end of the year. It also offered Australian governments and industry credits from its $1 billion Daybreak cyber defence fund. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks at the UN last week. Dominic Lorrimer The breach was prompted when the model was set a research task: to find government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities. When it could not find the figures, it took actions OpenAI “had not authorised it to take”, the company said.

Advertisement

OpenAI named three other agencies whose systems its models reached. At the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, a model used a public crime mapping tool that returned application configuration, operational jobs and logs. At the Victorian Department of Health, agents found an exposed access key and used it to query the Victorian Agency for Health Information’s reporting system. Attempts to bypass access controls failed at the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. OpenAI said no individual crime, medical or survey records were accessed in any of the incidents. Related Article Updated

AI OpenAI halts powerful new AI model over fears it could go rogue The company said it found the activity in mid-August, during a review prompted by a July breach at AI platform Hugging Face. It notified Services Australia and the Victorian Department of Health on September 10, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics on September 18 and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare on September 24. OpenAI said the institute’s case “did not meet our disclosure thresholds” because the access seemed consistent with public access. “We should have shared preliminary findings sooner and kept Australian agencies updated as more facts emerged,” it said.

Advertisement

Albanese said the incidents showed the risks of the technology, alongside its benefits for productivity, health and research. “There are risks, and we’ve seen those risks exposed not just in what occurred in Australia, but the revelation that has occurred in the United States and other countries as well,” he said on Tuesday. OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will fly in from the US to appear before parliament’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney on October 6, as this masthead reported on Monday. Anthropic will appear before the same committee that day. Neither company will appear at Thursday’s hearing of a separate Senate inquiry into AI and data centres. “We know we have a lot of work ahead of us to rebuild trust,” OpenAI said. title: Japan could redraw the global oil map
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsOil Opinion Japan could redraw the global oil map

Javier Blas September 29, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Among the world’s top fuel-consuming nations, Japan is the most energy insecure. Its import-dependency ratios are scary: It buys overseas 99.9 per cent of the oil it needs; 99.7 per cent of the coal; and 97.8 per cent of the natural gas. So Tokyo springs into action after every major energy shock to reassess its supply sources, making it a bellwether of global trends. The direction it’s signalling this time? Run away from the Middle East. Japan buys 99.9 per cent of the oil it needs from overseas, mostly from the Middle East. Time to reassess. Bloomberg Where Japan goes, others in Asia would too. Indeed, South Korea, another major energy importer, has already announced plans to reduce its reliance on the Middle East. India has been less vocal but was trying to diversify even before the war in Iran. Beyond creating a major conundrum for Middle Eastern suppliers, the shift goes against geographic, economic and historic reasoning.

Advertisement

The Middle East and Far East are relatively close, so it makes commercial sense — particularly when the cost of shipping is high, as it is now — that oil flows from one region to the other. And so it has done for decades. Despite its deep sense of energy vulnerability after the 1973-74 oil crisis, and again in 1979, Japan trusted the Middle East, buying more than 90 per cent of its crude from the region. With the benefit of hindsight, the policy was — to borrow a phrase from Nobuo Tanaka, a former senior energy official in Japan who later ran the International Energy Agency — a “mistake”. If the mantra in the 1970s and 1980s was ‘get oil out of electricity,’ the next objective should be more radical: get oil out of transportation. The official message is, of course, more diplomatic. But read between the lines, and it’s obvious that Japanese officials are trying to rectify what they see as a policy failure. The key is “diversifying procurement sources and transport routes”, according to a cabinet document. The goal, while unquantified, is clear: to “break free from a structural vulnerability where recurring energy supply instability and constraints act as a bottleneck for Japan’s economic growth”. To be sure, the documents also talk about supporting construction of new pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which would allow it to keep buying crude from, say, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia without having to worry as much about instability in Iran. But Japan still looks to be headed for a major supply shift.

Advertisement

The Japanese government is discussing the plan, and a formal announcement including import targets and taxpayer money to support it may come before year-end. Seoul, meanwhile, has already set a quota and vows to reduce its oil supply from any region to 50 per cent of the total. Currently, the Middle East accounts for just over 75 per cent of South Korean oil imports. Related Article Petrol prices Australian fuel prices near six-month highs on US-Iran peace deal impasse Japan may not have the numbers sorted, but it isn’t waiting for the end of the war to make changes. In July, according to the latest monthly data available, the US was its main provider of oil, accounting for 37 per cent of total petroleum imports. It’s worth repeating because it reflects the power of the US shale revolution along with the latest upheaval in the global oil market: Washington is today the biggest oil supplier to Tokyo. Mexico and Latin America provided another 3 per cent. Turning those one-off statistics into sustained flows won’t be easy. But if history serves as any guide, Japan has demonstrated it can shift its oil consumption when it senses its national security is at stake. Back in the late 1970s, the country consumed more than 5.5 million barrels a day, generating more than 60 per cent of its electricity burning crude and fuel-oil. Betting heavily on coal, nuclear and liquefied natural gas, it pushed oil out of its power industry almost entirely. By 2025, Japanese oil consumption had fallen to a 55-year low of less than 3 million barrels a day.

Advertisement

Reducing dependency on the Middle East would be easier if overall Japanese oil demand drops further. The fewer barrels it needs to buy, the easier it is to shift purchases. If the mantra in the 1970s and 1980s was “get oil out of electricity,” the next objective should be more radical: get oil out of transportation. Japan gave the world the first mass-produced hybrid car, Toyota’s Prius. But in terms of electric cars, it’s lagging countries like China. AP It was Japan that gave the world the first mass-produced hybrid car, Toyota’s Prius. Hybrids have made huge inroads since then, helping to reduce gasoline consumption by about half over the last two decades. But Japan, the world’s fourth-largest car market by sales totals, lags in adoption of pure electric vehicles. Having developed hybrids first, its car manufacturers didn’t push nearly as hard as China’s into full electrification. The result is that today only about 2 per cent of new cars sales in Japan are full EVs, well below the 28 per cent average in Europe, and even trailing the US and Canada. The International Energy Agency believes the high share of the population living in apartments with limited access to private parking, in combination with a limited charging network, are constraining EV sales in Japan. That makes EVs an important lever for reducing oil imports, which would make diversification easier. So alongside its plans to finance pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, Tokyo should work harder to boost EV sales, with a focus on expanding its EV charging infrastructure.

Advertisement

It also should try to reduce oil usage in heating. Rural Japan relies on kerosene stoves, an oddity among industrialised nations. If Tokyo manages to squeeze down its gasoline and kerosene demand, what would be left is diesel and other petrochemical feedstock. (As the world’s fourth-largest chemicals producer, it imports huge amounts of refined petroleum products used in plastics and other materials.) Related Article Exclusive

Blood Oil Funding Putin: ‘Blood oil’ imports from major Asian supplier surge The oil market’s algebra, however, is unyieldingly zero-sum. If Japan succeeds, it will have to elbow its way into markets others consider their own, like West Africa and the Americas, the traditional hunting grounds of European refiners. And producers in the Middle East would need to find new customers. Trouble is, who would like to boost its reliance on Middle Eastern oil? I draw a blank. That wouldn’t be Tokyo’s problem to solve. But it’s another way in which Japan could change the global oil map for good.

Three years after it was mothballed, national brick maker Brickworks will restart operations at its Austral Bricks facility in Cardup, south of Perth, with the help of taxpayers. The state government will spend $4 million to restart operations at the Cardup plant and boost brick production in WA by 10 to 15 per cent in a bid to address the state’s crippling shortage, which has home builders fearing for their futures. WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti. Ross Swanborough The money will include a $3 million payment to Brickworks to recommission equipment at the Cardup site as well as a $500,000 payment to ensure the plant resumes operations by March. Another $500,000 payment will be made if Brickworks can deliver 17 million maxibricks – which are used in internal walls and general construction – within the first year of operations.

Advertisement

Perth home builders have been warning the state government for months of a looming a brick shortage in the state after Midland Brick began rationing bricks. “This is a time where we can’t allow this situation to roll on without doing anything,” Treasurer Rita Saffioti said on Tuesday. “Something needs to be done. We see the urgency. The building industry, in particular, have been very clear. “We need to get more bricks as soon as possible to ensure this doesn’t become a major challenge that exists for years upon years.” Even the state’s biggest builders like Dale Alcock of the ABN Group are struggling to get bricks to service their huge pipeline of work

Advertisement

Advertisement

He said 17 million maxibricks was the capacity of the plant, which it was running at in 2021-22. Ellenor said the March timeframe was tight but achievable, and they had already deployed engineers and operations staff from the East Coast to start the recommissioning. “The time frame is tight but all going well we will have bricks being produced in late March. The main challenge will be employing 35 workers in the Byford area,” he said. Alcock said he would go as far as to say that Brickworks’ new facility would still not produce enough bricks to meet demand, “but it’s certainly a large help.” The state government has poured about $100 million into boosting alternative construction methods to reduce the state’s obsession with double brick.

Advertisement

However, Alcock said WA was still a double brick state. “We talk about different methods of construction. We’re up for that, but you can’t just change your construction methodology overnight as an industry,” he said. “I encourage the government to undertake whatever support they can to Midland Brick and to Brickworks to try and increase capacity over the coming years because we are a double brick state and we need bricks.” Alcock said his company had about 100 jobs with slabs down, but no bricks loaded on them. “It’s taking us about an average of about four to six weeks to get brick supply,” he said.

Advertisement

Housing Industry Association WA boss Michael McGowan said 70 per cent of homes in the state were built using the double brick construction method. He said there would likely still be delays over the next 12 months and asked customers to be patient with builders and trades. Home Builders Action Group chairman Jason Janssen has been raising the industries concerns for months and said, while he welcomed the news that Cardup was restarting, it wouldn’t be enough. “It gives us hope from March to next year but between now and then there is a lot of uncertainty,” he said. Janssen called on the state government to switch the majority of its public housing build program, which includes thousands of dwellings, from double brick to alternative construction methods to free up bricks in the private market.

title: AFL considering changes to free agency system
text:

Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 AFL considering changes to free agency system Jake Niall Updated September 29, 2026 — 1:52pm ,first published 12:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL will consider changes to free agency in the interests of ensuring that the system does not skew the competitive balance of the competition in favour of the teams in premiership contention. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon confirmed that the league would discuss potential changes to the free agency rules to make sure that the competitive balance of the 18 clubs was not distorted. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon has flagged potential changes to free agency. Eddie Jim “Look, I think it’s been in place for now probably 12 or 14 years,” the AFL boss told this masthead in grand final week. “I think what we’re seeing in the last couple of years is what everyone thought would happen at the start, and it didn’t necessarily. “But it’s something that we’ll talk with the players association about because competitive balance is really important. That you know, we do a lot of work around the draft, we do a lot of work around the salary cap, a lot of work around the soft cap.”

Advertisement

Asked if the AFL would consider changes to free agency, Dillon said: “Yeah, with the agreement [with the players], just to make sure that the competitive balance isn’t distorted.” The potential to reform free agency – which was introduced for 2012 and has been the subject of minor changes and ongoing debate – comes as the Brisbane Lions, once stragglers, won their third flag on end in their fourth consecutive grand final. They attracted both Sam Draper and Oscar Allen from lowly Essendon and West Coast, respectively, as free agents, albeit the Eagles received a generous pick No.2 for their ex-skipper. The AFL wanted to change the compensation system at the end of last year to remove compensation picks inside the top 10, and thus not compromise the draft for teams who weren’t finalists (not counting the new wildcards). But the AFL Players’ Association resisted that change, and the status quo remained. As a result, Port Adelaide can receive pick No.5 in return for departing superstar free agent Zak Butters and Gold Coast can gain pick No.7 for key forward Ben King, who is crossing to Hawthorn.

Advertisement

These deals give the clubs losing the star arguably superior compensation compared to what they could gain in a trade if they choose to match the free agent offers. The AFL is closely watching the side deals that those clubs – the Western Bulldogs and Port, Hawthorn and Gold Coast – propose, to make sure that they are “commercial” and reflect market value. Related Article Opinion

AFL grand final Why three-peat Hawks and another super side have Fagan’s Heroes covered Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age One potential reform, which is likely to be canvassed, is a rule that forces the top teams to give up a draft pick, such as their first pick, for a high-value free agent. Under that reform, Hawthorn, as a top four team, would lose their first draft pick for King, and still land him as a free agent. This could potentially apply to the top four, top six or top eight teams from that season. Most of the most prized free agents have gone to teams that had been in premiership contention. These include Lance Franklin (Sydney), Patrick Dangerfield (Geelong), Tom Lynch (Richmond), Jeremy Cameron (Geelong) and Joe Daniher (Brisbane Lions). It is rare for a restricted free agent to opt for a team in the bottom six or eight. Older superstars Lachie Neale and Toby Greene are joining Collingwood and Geelong respectively as unrestricted free agents this year.

Advertisement

The position on free agency varies among clubs. Some would argue that it should be less restricted, others that the system is skewed towards teams in premiership contention. AFL free agency is enshrined in the players’ collective bargaining agreement and needs the players’ union’s consent to be altered in that agreement. The union has consistently opposed any measures that impede the ability of players to cross to their preferred club after a period of service. “The current free agency parameters mean only a small number of players take advantage of it each year. That makes it very competitive to attract free agents that become available,” AFLPA boss James Gallagher said. “Choice of club is important for players with relatively short career spans who don’t choose where their careers start. “Free agency has a role in competitive balance but that needs to be considered alongside other factors like the draft and its compromises, other player movement mechanisms and the soft cap.
